course.title: Linux and the Command Line
course.description: Learn to read and write command lines, join small programs with pipes, and understand permissions, processes and services well enough to work on a real Linux machine.
course.audience: A capable adult who uses a computer daily and has met files and programs but not a terminal. Assumes the CS Basics idea of a precise procedure and, from How Computers and Networks Work, the lessons on memory and storage and on processes and the kernel. Git and Version Control assumes the first two lessons here.

paragraphs: A Linux machine is controlled, in the end, by lines of text. A line such as ls -l /etc names a program and gives it words to work on, a program called the shell splits the line into those words and starts the program, and the program reads text and writes text. Because every program follows that one convention, the output of one command can be handed to the next, and a few small tools joined together do work that none of them could do alone.

The rest of the system can be read in the same way. A file is found by its place in a single tree of directories, the permission to read or change it is recorded as a short pattern of letters on the file itself, and every running program is a process with an owner that can be listed and stopped. A service writes its messages to logs that print as text, so a question such as who is allowed to change a file, or why a service stopped, can be answered by running a command and reading what it prints.

A command that deletes or overwrites a file acts the moment you press Enter, and rm does not send anything to a rubbish bin, so it pays to work out what a line will do before you run it. Because commands are text, they can also be saved in a file and run again unchanged, and a task done once by hand can then be repeated by a script or started on a schedule.
outcomes: You'll be able to read a command line and say what each word does.
You'll be able to navigate and change the file tree with absolute and relative paths.
You'll be able to join commands with pipes to count, filter and summarise text.
You'll be able to read and set permissions in octal and symbolic form.
You'll be able to explain what a process, a signal and an environment variable are.
You'll be able to read a short shell script and predict its output and exit status.
introduction.prerequisites: You should know the idea of a precise procedure from How Computers Solve Problems, and the lessons on memory and storage and on processes and the kernel from How Computers and Networks Work. No experience of a terminal is needed.

modules.title: Working in the shell
modules.description: What a command is, how the file tree is laid out, and how to look at, change and link files.

modules.title: Text, streams and pipelines
modules.description: Programs that read and write text, joined by pipes, with search, patterns and transformation.

modules.title: Permissions, processes and scripts
modules.description: Who may do what, what is running, how a command finds its settings, and how to keep a sequence of commands in a script.

concepts.title: Shell
concepts.summary: A program that reads a line you type, splits it into words, and starts the program named by the first word.

concepts.title: Argument and option
concepts.summary: Every word after the program name is passed to it as a separate argument; options are arguments that begin with a dash and change what the program does.

concepts.title: Manual page
concepts.summary: The reference document for a command, organised into numbered sections and read with man.

concepts.title: Path
concepts.summary: A string of directory names separated by slashes that names one file; it is absolute if it begins with / and otherwise relative to the current directory.

concepts.title: Working directory
concepts.summary: The directory a process is currently in, which relative paths are resolved against.

concepts.title: Filesystem hierarchy
concepts.summary: The conventional layout in which /etc holds configuration, /var holds changing data such as logs, /home holds users' files and /usr holds installed programs.

concepts.title: Long listing
concepts.summary: The output of ls -l: type and permissions, link count, owner, group, size in bytes, modification time and name.

concepts.title: Lines, words and bytes
concepts.summary: wc counts newline characters, whitespace-separated words, and bytes, which can differ from the number of characters.

concepts.title: Pager
concepts.summary: A program such as less that shows a file one screen at a time and lets you search it.

concepts.title: Glob
concepts.summary: A pattern containing * (any run of characters), ? (exactly one character) or [ ] (one from a set) that the shell expands to matching file names before the program starts.

concepts.title: Quoting
concepts.summary: Single quotes pass text exactly, double quotes keep it as one word but still allow $ expansion, and a backslash escapes one character.

concepts.title: Destructive commands
concepts.summary: rm and overwriting redirection remove data immediately, with no rubbish bin to recover from.

concepts.title: Inode
concepts.summary: The record that holds a file's metadata and the location of its data; a directory entry is a name that points at an inode.

concepts.title: Hard link and symbolic link
concepts.summary: A hard link is another name for the same inode; a symbolic link is a small file that stores a path and breaks if the target is removed.

concepts.title: Mount
concepts.summary: Attaching a filesystem to a directory so that its contents appear in the tree at that point.

concepts.title: Standard streams
concepts.summary: Every process starts with input (descriptor 0), output (1) and error (2).

concepts.title: Redirection
concepts.summary: > sends output to a file and truncates it, >> appends, < reads input from a file, and 2> redirects the error stream.

concepts.title: Pipe
concepts.summary: The | operator connects one command's standard output to the next command's standard input, running both at once.

concepts.title: grep
concepts.summary: Prints the lines of its input that match a pattern; -c counts them, -v inverts, -n numbers them, -i ignores case and -r searches a tree.

concepts.title: find
concepts.summary: Walks a directory tree and tests each entry by name, type, size or age.

concepts.title: Search exit status
concepts.summary: grep exits 0 when it found a match, 1 when it found none and 2 on error.

concepts.title: Regular expression
concepts.summary: A compact pattern describing a set of strings, built from literal characters and operators.

concepts.title: Anchor
concepts.summary: ^ matches the start of a line and $ the end, so a pattern with both must match the whole line.

concepts.title: Character class and repetition
concepts.summary: [a-z] matches one character from a set, . matches any one character, and * + ? {n} say how many times the previous item repeats.

concepts.title: Sort order
concepts.summary: sort orders lines as text by default, so 100 comes before 9, and sort -n orders them as numbers.

concepts.title: Field
concepts.summary: A part of a line separated by a delimiter; cut -d, -f2 and awk -F, '{print $2}' take the second one.

concepts.title: Count pipeline
concepts.summary: sort | uniq -c | sort -rn is the standard way to count how often each value occurs and rank them.

concepts.title: Mode
concepts.summary: Nine permission bits: read, write and execute for the owner, the group and everyone else, written rwx or as three octal digits where r=4, w=2, x=1.

concepts.title: Directory permissions
concepts.summary: Read lets you list names, write lets you create and remove entries, and execute lets you pass through the directory to reach what is inside.

concepts.title: umask
concepts.summary: The bits removed from the default mode of new files (666) and directories (777).

concepts.title: Process ID and parent
concepts.summary: Every process has a number (PID) and a parent that started it; PID 1 starts the rest.

concepts.title: Signal
concepts.summary: A short numbered message sent to a process; SIGTERM (15) asks it to finish, SIGKILL (9) cannot be caught, SIGINT (2) is what Ctrl-C sends and SIGHUP (1) means the terminal closed.

concepts.title: Exit status
concepts.summary: The number a process returns when it ends: 0 means success and any other value means failure.

concepts.title: Shell variable
concepts.summary: A named string set with name=value and read with $name; it exists only in that shell until exported.

concepts.title: Environment
concepts.summary: The exported variables copied from a process to each child it starts.

concepts.title: Script
concepts.summary: A text file of shell commands, begun with a #! line naming the interpreter and made executable.

concepts.title: Conditional chain
concepts.summary: cmd1 && cmd2 runs cmd2 only if cmd1 succeeded and cmd1 || cmd2 only if it failed; if tests the exit status of a command.

concepts.title: Positional parameters
concepts.summary: $1, $2 and so on hold the arguments, $# their count and "$@" all of them as separate words.

concepts.title: Package manager
concepts.summary: A tool such as apt or dnf that installs software and its dependencies from signed repositories and tracks what is installed.

concepts.title: Service and unit
concepts.summary: A long-running program managed by systemd through a unit file; systemctl start runs it now and enable runs it at boot.

concepts.title: Journal
concepts.summary: The systemd log store, read with journalctl; -u selects one unit.

lessons.title: The shell and a command

steps.headline: A command line is a program name followed by arguments, and some of those arguments are options that change what the program does.

lead.text: Take the line ls -l /etc. It has three words separated by blanks, and each one has a different job. The first word, ls, names the **program** that will run. Every word after it is handed to that program as a separate **argument**, which is the program's own input: here -l and /etc.

The two arguments are not alike. /etc is the thing ls is to work on, a directory. -l begins with a dash, and an argument of that kind is called an **option**, because it changes what the program does without being the thing it works on. With -l, ls prints one detailed line per file in place of a bare list of names. The figure marks the three roles in colour, and its second view shows a line with more than one plain argument.

afterFigure.text: Notice that -l is not part of the program's name. ls -l is the same program as ls, started with one extra argument, and the program reads that argument and decides what to print. Any word after the first is an argument; the dash is only a convention that marks the ones a program treats as options.

diagram.alt: A command line split into boxes. In ls -l /etc, ls is the program, -l an option and /etc an argument. A second view shows cp -r src dst, where the three words after cp are all arguments.
diagram.caption: Colour marks the role of each word. Use the buttons to compare two lines.

reveal.text: The next screen shows what the program receives. The answer is the number of separate words after the program name, however many blanks lay between them.

steps.headline: The shell reads the line, splits it at runs of blanks, finds the program named by the first word and starts it.

lead.text: You do not type into the program directly. The window you type in is a **terminal**, which only displays text and carries your keystrokes, and it passes each line to a separate program called the **shell**. The shell does the work of a command line: it splits the line into words, uses the first word to find a program, starts that program as a new process with the other words as its arguments, waits for it to finish, and then prints the prompt again.

Splitting happens at blanks, and a run of blanks counts as a single boundary. In echo one  two   three the gaps are one, two and three spaces wide, yet the program receives exactly three arguments, one, two and three. You can check it with set -- one  two   three; echo $#, which prints 3. The extra blanks were information for the shell only, and the figure shows what survives.

afterFigure.text: That is why spacing never changes what a command means, provided the words stay apart. It is also why the shell and the terminal are not the same thing: the terminal could be replaced by another window and the shell would run unchanged. The first Unix shell was written by Ken Thompson in the early 1970s, and Bash, the GNU project's shell and the one this course uses, was first released in 1989.

diagram.alt: Two views of the line echo one  two   three. The first shows the line as typed with gaps of one, two and three blanks. The second shows echo receiving three arguments, one, two and three, with no gaps.
diagram.caption: The shell uses blanks only to find where words end, so the program receives the words and nothing else.

reveal.text: The terminal window only displays text. The program that splits the line and starts the command is the shell.

steps.headline: Options are arguments that start with a dash, and single-letter options may be written together after one dash.

lead.text: Most commands come with a list of options. A **short option** is a dash and one letter, such as -l or -a, and a **long option** is two dashes and a word, such as --all. In ls, -a and --all mean the same thing: show the entries whose names begin with a dot, which the listing leaves out otherwise.

Short options can usually be combined. ls -l -a asks for the long format and for all entries, and ls -la asks for exactly the same, since the program reads each letter after a single dash as its own option. This is a convention that most commands follow, not a rule of the shell, because the shell passes -la on as one unbroken word and leaves ls to take it apart.

afterFigure.text: Long options cost more typing and are easier to read in a script, since --all says what it does where -a has to be remembered. Some options also take a value of their own, as in head -n 2, where 2 belongs to -n; a later lesson uses that form.

steps.headline: Read sort -rn scores.txt: find the program, the options and the argument.

workedSteps.text: The first word names the program, so sort is the program that runs.
The second word starts with a dash, so it is an option, and it holds two letters, r and n. For this program that means the same as the two separate options -r and -n.
The last word has no dash. It is the name of the file for sort to work on, so it is a plain argument.
The shell hands sort two arguments, -rn and scores.txt, and starts the process.

steps.headline: Count the arguments in ls -l -a /home /tmp, then compare with the line ls -la /home /tmp.

workedSteps.text: Split the line at its blanks. The first word, ls, names the program.
Every remaining word is passed on. Write them down: -l, -a, /home and /tmp.
ls receives -l, -a, /home and /tmp. Work out how many arguments that is.

steps.headline: The manual is divided into numbered sections, and the same name can have a page in more than one of them.

lead.text: Nobody remembers every option of every command, so the system carries its own reference. A page of it is called a **manual page**, and you read one with the man command: man ls opens the page for ls. Pages are grouped into numbered **sections**. Section 1 holds commands, section 5 holds file formats, and section 8 holds administration commands, with the others given in the figure.

The same word can appear in more than one section. passwd is a command that changes a password, described in section 1, and it is also the name of the account file /etc/passwd, described in section 5. Typing man passwd shows the first match, so to read the other you give the section before the name: man 5 passwd. The usual written form of the name includes the section, as in passwd(5).

afterFigure.text: A manual page is a reference rather than a lesson, and it is laid out the same way every time: a name, a synopsis showing how the command is written, a description, and a list of options. When you do not know which section to open, the table of sections tells you which kind of page you are after.

reveal.text: The section for file formats holds the page for /etc/passwd, which man 5 passwd opens.
Commands meant for the administrator are kept apart from commands every user runs, so man 8 useradd and man 1 passwd name different shelves.

lessons.orientation: Read a command line as a program name followed by options and arguments, and say how the shell splits it.
lessons.nextAction: Move around the file tree with absolute and relative paths, and say where on a Linux system a given kind of file belongs.

blocks.text: The line ls -l /etc, typed at a prompt, makes the system print one detailed line for every file in the /etc directory. It is made of three words, and each does a different job: ls is the name of a program, -l asks that program for its long listing, and /etc names the directory to list. Change the last word to /tmp and the same program lists another place, and leave out the second word and the detail disappears.

Every command line is built the same way, so once you can say what each word does, you can say what the line will do before you press Enter, and a line you have never seen before becomes one you can check. When a word is unfamiliar, the system carries its own manual, which describes what each command accepts.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to split a command line into its program, options and arguments, and to open the manual section that describes a command or a file.
intro.whyItMatters: Every later lesson is built from command lines, and a line you can read is a line you can check before running it.

recap.keyIdea: A command line is a program name followed by arguments, which the shell splits at blanks before it starts the program.

blocks.text: The shell reads your line, treats each run of blanks as one boundary, and starts the program named by the first word with the remaining words as its arguments. Options are arguments that begin with a dash, and for most commands single-letter options can be joined, so ls -la means ls -l -a.
When you need to know what a command accepts, the manual page holds the answer, and the section number in front of the name, as in man 5 passwd, picks the right page when one name belongs to several.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at where files live, so that the arguments you type can name places on the system.

lessons.title: Files and the filesystem tree

steps.headline: Every file sits in one tree that starts at /, and a path names a place in it either from the root or from where you stand.

lead.text: A Linux system keeps all of its files in a single tree. At the top is a directory called the **root**, written /, and every other directory sits below it, so there are no drive letters as on some other systems. A file or directory is named by a **path**, which is a list of directory names separated by slashes, ending at the thing you want: /home/ana/docs is the directory docs, inside ana, inside home, inside the root.

A path that begins with / is an **absolute path**, because it starts from the root and means the same wherever you are. A path with no leading slash is a **relative path**, and it starts from the **working directory**, the directory your shell is currently in. From /home/ana the relative path docs names the same place as /home/ana/docs. The figure shows both ways of naming one directory.

afterFigure.text: The working directory is why a short name works at all. The shell keeps it for you, and every command you start begins in it. The command pwd prints it, and cd changes it to the directory you name.

reveal.text: The next screen explains the two special names, . and .., that make this possible.

steps.headline: The name . means the directory you are in, .. means its parent, and a leading ~ is replaced by your home directory.

lead.text: Every directory contains two entries that the system maintains for you. The name . stands for the directory itself, and **..** stands for its **parent directory**, the one that holds it. Because they are ordinary names, they can be strung together: ../.. is the parent of the parent. A path built this way depends only on the tree and on where you stand, never on the places you visited before.

A leading ~ is different, since it is not stored in the filesystem at all. The shell replaces it, before it starts the command, with the path of your home directory, so ~/docs becomes something like /home/ana/docs. Follow the figure, which takes the command cd ../../etc from /var/log one .. at a time. Each .. removes a name from the end of the path, and the final name is entered from wherever that leaves you.

steps.headline: Trace cd ../../etc from /var/log, one name at a time.

workedSteps.text: The working directory is /var/log, a path of two names below the root.
The first .. removes the last name. What the .. stands for is the parent directory.
The second .. removes another name, which leaves only the root.
The last part, etc, is a name inside the root, so it is added.
pwd now prints the new working directory.

steps.headline: Trace cd ../../bo/notes from /home/ana/projects.

workedSteps.text: The working directory is /home/ana/projects, a path of three names.
The two .. remove projects and then ana, which leaves /home.
The names bo and notes are then added in turn. Write the path that pwd prints.

steps.headline: The top level of the tree follows a standard layout, so you can tell from a path what kind of file it holds.

lead.text: Nobody decides again, system by system, where logs or settings go. The Filesystem Hierarchy Standard sets out the conventional layout, and most Linux systems follow it closely. **/etc** holds configuration files, the settings that an administrator edits. **/var** holds data that changes while the system runs, with logs under /var/log. **/usr** holds installed programs and their libraries, the programs themselves often in /usr/bin, and **/home** holds each person's own files.

Two more are worth knowing. /tmp is for temporary files and may be emptied at any time, so nothing there should be the only copy of anything. /proc is not a folder of stored files at all: it is a window onto the kernel, whose entries, such as /proc/cpuinfo, are made up when you read them to describe the processor and the running processes. The standard grew out of an effort for Linux in 1994, and version 3.0 was released in 2015.

afterFigure.text: A path therefore carries meaning. Seeing /etc/ in front of a file name tells you it is a setting, and seeing /var/log/ tells you it is a record of something that happened. When you are unsure where something belongs, ask what kind of file it is, and the top-level directory follows.

diagram.alt: Six top-level directories drawn as tiles: etc for configuration, var for data that changes, usr for installed programs, home for people's files, tmp for temporary files and proc for running processes. A second view gives an example path under each.

steps.headline: A name that begins with a dot is skipped by plain ls, and that is a convention rather than a protection.

lead.text: Programs keep their own settings for you in files in your home directory, and so many are needed that they would crowd every listing. The convention is that **a name beginning with a dot is left out of ls by default**. A file called .bashrc is therefore invisible to ls and visible to ls -a, whose -a stands for all. The file is not protected or special in any other way: you can read it, edit it and delete it like any other.

The same option shows . and .., the two entries that every directory holds. A directory containing only notes.txt and .hidden therefore prints a single name for ls, and four for ls -a: ., .., .hidden and notes.txt. Hidden is a convenient word, but all that has happened is that ls chose not to print some names.

reveal.text: The option -a adds every name that begins with a dot, including the two that every directory holds, to the two files, so all four names are printed.

lessons.orientation: Navigate with absolute and relative paths and say where on a Linux system a given kind of file belongs.
lessons.nextAction: Look inside files: read the columns of a long listing and view a file with cat, head, tail, wc and less.

blocks.text: Type pwd in a terminal and it prints a single line, perhaps /home/ana. The line is a path, a list of directory names joined by slashes, and it says exactly where the shell is standing in the tree of files: the first slash is the top of the tree, home is a directory directly below it, and ana is a directory inside home.

Almost every command takes paths as arguments, so reading them is as basic as reading the command itself. A path also tells you what you are looking at, because the layout of the tree is standard: a file under /etc is a setting, one under /var/log is a record of events, and one under /home is somebody's own. With that you can say where a command will act, and what kind of file it will touch, before you press Enter.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to work out where a relative path leads, and to say in which top-level directory a given kind of file belongs.
intro.whyItMatters: A path you can resolve is a path you can check before running a command that changes something.

recap.keyIdea: A path names a place in the one tree that starts at /, either from the root or relative to the working directory, and the standard layout tells you what each top-level directory holds.

blocks.text: An absolute path begins with / and means the same wherever you are, while a relative path starts from the working directory, with . for here and .. for the parent. Following a path means removing one name for each .. and adding the names after it, and a leading ~ is replaced by the shell with your home directory.
The standard layout puts settings in /etc, data that changes in /var, programs in /usr and personal files in /home, and ls leaves out names that begin with a dot unless it is given -a.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson uses these paths to look inside files: their size, their type, and their contents.

lessons.title: Looking at files

steps.headline: A long listing gives one line per file, and each field of the line answers a separate question about it.

lead.text: Plain ls prints only names. Add the option -l and it prints a **long listing**, with one line for each file and several fields of information on that line. For a file named report.txt the line might read -rw-r--r-- 1 ana staff 2048 Mar 3 10:12 report.txt, and the fields run in a fixed order: the type and permissions, a count of names the file has, its owner, its group, its size, the time it was last changed, and its name.

The first character of the first field gives the type, which is a dash for an ordinary file, d for a directory and l for a symbolic link. The nine characters after it are the permissions, which a later lesson reads in full. The size is in **bytes**, the unit in which a computer counts stored data, so the figure of 2048 means two thousand and forty-eight bytes, not kilobytes, unless you add -h to the option, which prints a rounded size such as 2.0K.

afterFigure.text: Most of these fields come up again in later lessons: the link count when we meet links, and the permissions, owner and group when we reach access. For now the useful skill is to find the field you need, since the size and the time are what you will check most often.

steps.headline: cat prints a whole file, head prints its first lines and tail its last, and the option -n sets how many.

lead.text: The simplest way to see what a file holds is cat, which prints all of it. That is fine for a few lines and wrong for a large file, because the beginning scrolls past before you can read it. head prints only the first lines, ten by default, and tail prints the last ten. The option -n changes the number, so head -n 2 notes.txt prints two lines and tail -n 2 notes.txt prints two.

The figure shows the file notes.txt as five numbered rows, which hold alpha, beta, gamma, delta and epsilon. You can think of head and tail as a window laid over those rows: head puts it at the start, tail at the end, and the option -n says how many rows the window holds. Everything outside the window is dropped from the output, and the file itself is left as it was.

afterFigure.text: Reading the end of a file is the commoner job than it sounds, because logs and other records grow by adding lines at the bottom, so the newest entries are the last ones. tail is how you see what has just happened.

steps.headline: Taking head and then tail with | between them picks out one line of a file by its position.

lead.text: A bar between two commands is called a **pipe**, and it hands the output of the left-hand command to the right-hand one as its input. A later lesson explains pipes properly, but one use is already worth having. To read the second line of a file, ask head for the first two lines and let tail keep the last of them: head -n 2 notes.txt | tail -n 1. The window of the second command is laid over the output of the first, and not over the file.

Reading from the other end works the same way. tail -n 2 notes.txt passes on delta and epsilon, and head -n 1 keeps the first of those, which is delta. The general rule is that to pick line n you take the first n lines and keep the last one of them, and the figure shows two of the combinations.

afterFigure.text: Notice that the order matters. Swapping the two commands in the first pipeline gives tail -n 2 notes.txt | head -n 1, which prints delta and not beta.

diagram.alt: The five lines of notes.txt as numbered rows. For head -n 2 followed by tail -n 1, rows 1 and 2 are passed on and row 2, beta, is kept. For tail -n 2 followed by head -n 1, rows 4 and 5 are passed on and row 4, delta, is kept.

steps.headline: wc counts newline characters, words and bytes, so its line count can fall one short of the lines you can read.

lead.text: The command wc, for word count, reports three numbers for a file: the lines, the words and the bytes. For notes.txt, wc notes.txt prints 5 5 31, and the options -l, -w and -c choose one of them. A **newline** is the invisible character that ends each line, and it is stored in the file like a letter, as one byte. The five words of notes.txt hold 26 letters, and the five newlines bring the byte count to 31.

wc -l does not count the lines you see; it counts the newline characters. A file whose last line has no newline after it therefore reports one line less than a person would count, since that last line is never ended. Files made by most programs finish every line, so the difference is rare, but it does mean a count can be one off. The form wc -c < notes.txt, which feeds the file to wc without naming it, prints the number alone, where wc -c notes.txt would add the file name.

steps.headline: Work out wc -c for notes.txt line by line, and check the total against 31.

workedSteps.text: Each line is one word plus its newline. The word alpha has five letters.
beta has four letters, and gamma and delta have five each.
epsilon has seven letters.
Adding the five line totals gives the byte count.

steps.headline: Find the third line of notes.txt with head and tail, in two steps.

workedSteps.text: The window of head -n 3 covers the first three lines.
tail -n 1 then keeps the last line of what head passed on.
Work out which line of notes.txt the pipeline prints.

steps.headline: less shows a file one screen at a time, which suits any file too long to read at once.

lead.text: When a file is longer than the screen, cat floods the window and head or tail shows only one end of it. A **pager** is a program that displays a file one screen at a time, and the usual one is less. Run less on a file and it opens at the top: space moves down a screen, b moves back up, and a slash followed by a word searches forward for it, with n jumping to the next match.

To leave, press q. less does not read the whole file before it displays it, so even a log with millions of lines opens at once. The name is a joke on an older pager called more, which could only move forward.

reveal.text: The key q ends less. The other keys only move around inside the file or search it.
Printing the file would show three lines, and wc -l reports two, so a count of lines and the number of lines you can read are not always the same thing.

lessons.orientation: Inspect a file's size, type and contents with ls -l, cat, head, tail, wc and less, and read the columns of a long listing.
lessons.nextAction: Create, copy, move and delete files, and predict what globs and quotes will expand to before a command runs.

blocks.text: The line -rw-r--r-- 1 ana staff 2048 Mar 3 10:12 report.txt says a good deal about a file before you open it: it is an ordinary file, ana owns it, it holds 2048 bytes, and it was last changed on 3 March at 10:12. Each fact sits in a fixed place in the line, so the size or the date of any file in a directory can be found by looking in the same place on its line.

The next question is what the file holds, and the right way to look depends on how much there is. A configuration file can be a dozen lines and a log can be a million, so a command that prints everything suits the first and buries what you want in the second. Knowing how to look at the start of a file, at its end, at its size, or at one screen at a time lets you read the file in front of you without losing the part that matters.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read the fields of a long listing, pick out a line of a file by its position, and say what wc will count.
intro.whyItMatters: The size, time and contents of a file are usually the first things to check before you act on it.

recap.keyIdea: A long listing answers questions about a file before you open it, and head, tail, wc and less show you as much of its contents as you need.

blocks.text: The long listing gives the type and permissions, links, owner, group, size in bytes, time of last change and name, and ls -l counts the size in bytes. head and tail take a window from either end of a file, and joining them with a pipe picks out one line by its position, as in head -n 2 notes.txt | tail -n 1.
wc counts newline characters, words and bytes, so a last line with no newline is missed by wc -l, and less is the command for reading a file too long for one screen.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson stops reading and starts changing files: creating, copying, moving and deleting them, and the patterns the shell expands before the command runs.

lessons.title: Changing files

steps.headline: Four commands make, copy, rename and delete files, and rm leaves nothing behind to recover.

lead.text: A directory is made with mkdir, and mkdir -p builds a whole chain of directories at once. An empty file is made with touch, which sets the file's modification time and creates the file when the name is new. Copying uses cp, as in cp a.txt b.txt, which leaves a.txt and adds a second file b.txt with the same content. A copied directory needs the option -r, which stands for recursive and copies everything beneath it.

Moving uses mv, and a move within one directory is the way to rename: mv a.txt b.txt leaves a single file under the new name. rm deletes. The figure shows what each of the three leaves in a directory that held only a.txt, so that the end state of each command is clear before you run it.

afterFigure.text: A directory is removed with rmdir when it is empty, and rm -r removes it together with everything inside. The commands mean what they say and ask nothing, which matters in the next screens.

diagram.alt: Three before and after views of a directory that holds a.txt. After cp a.txt b.txt it holds a.txt and b.txt. After mv a.txt b.txt it holds only b.txt. After rm a.txt it is empty.

There is no rubbish bin to fetch it from.</text></svg>

reveal.text: The next screen says what the commands do to data that already exists, and shows why the answer matters.

steps.headline: rm and mv replace or remove data at once, because the shell has no rubbish bin and asks for nothing by default.

lead.text: The answer to the last question is that mv replaces the target without comment. This is the first of two kinds of **destructive command**, one that removes or overwrites data at once. A file removed with rm is not sent to a rubbish bin, since the shell has none, and an existing file replaced by mv or by a copy with cp is lost in the same way. Redirecting output into an existing file, which a later lesson covers, does the same.

The options -i, for interactive, makes cp, mv and rm ask before replacing or removing, and it is worth typing whenever the target might already exist. A further habit is to check before you delete: replace rm with ls in the same line to see what a pattern would remove, and then change it back. A line such as rm -rf with a variable that turned out to be empty can remove far more than you meant, which is why the next topic, how patterns are expanded, comes first.

steps.headline: A pattern is replaced by the matching names before the command starts, so the program never sees the pattern.

lead.text: Typing every file name by hand would be slow, so the shell lets you write a pattern, called a **glob**, and replaces it by the names that match. A star * matches any run of characters, including none, a question mark ? matches exactly one character, and a pair of brackets such as [1-2] matches one character from the set between them. A glob is written where an argument would be, as in ls file*.txt.

The shell does this work, not the program. Before it starts ls it looks in the directory, finds the matching names, sorts them and puts them in place of the pattern, so ls receives an argument list of file names. In a directory holding file1.txt, file2.txt and file10.txt, the pattern file?.txt matches two names, because 10 is two characters, file*.txt matches all three, and file[1-2].txt matches two.

afterFigure.text: Since the program sees only the result, it can never tell that you typed a pattern. If nothing matches, the shell leaves the pattern as it was, and the program receives the literal text, star and all.

reveal.text: The brackets match one character, so the longer name never qualifies. The two shorter names do.
The next screen shows how quotes change the answer, by keeping a blank inside a single word.

steps.headline: Quotes keep a blank, a star or a dollar sign from being treated as syntax, so one name arrives as one word.

lead.text: The shell finds words by blanks and expands patterns by stars, which is a problem when you want those characters to mean themselves. **Quoting** switches that interpretation off. Single quotes pass everything inside them exactly as written. Double quotes keep what is inside as one word but still allow a dollar sign to start a variable, a feature that a later lesson uses. A backslash in front of one character switches off the meaning of that single character.

So touch my file creates two files, my and file, while touch "my file" creates one whose name contains a space. A quoted star is no longer a glob either: ls '*.txt' looks for a file whose name is literally *.txt. The figure shows the two ways of typing the first example, and the number of arguments is what differs.

afterFigure.text: Quote any name that might contain a blank, and quote a star you want kept as a star. The simplest safe habit is to quote names whenever you are not sure they contain only letters, digits and a few punctuation marks.

diagram.alt: Two views of a line. Typed without quotes, touch my file gives touch two arguments, my and file, and creates two files. Typed as touch followed by my file in double quotes, it gives touch one argument and creates one file with a space in its name.

reveal.text: The pattern is passed on as typed, because the shell found no names to put in its place. Many scripts have a bug of this kind when a directory is empty.

lessons.orientation: Create, copy, move and delete files and directories, and predict what globs and quotes will expand to before a command runs.
lessons.nextAction: Say what a file name really is, how a hard link differs from a symbolic link, and how a second disk joins the tree.

blocks.text: Type echo *.txt in a directory that holds notes.txt and plan.txt, and the line prints notes.txt plan.txt. The echo command never saw the star: before it started, the shell looked in the directory, replaced the pattern with the names that matched, and handed echo those two names as its arguments. A program receives only the result of the pattern, so the words it gets are not always the words you typed.

That matters most for the commands that create, copy, move and delete files, which are short and act at once. Knowing which words the program will receive tells you what the command will do, and when you want the shell to leave a word alone, whether it is a pattern or a name with a blank in it, you put it in quotes.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say which names a pattern matches, how many arguments a quoted or unquoted name becomes, and which commands replace data without asking.
intro.whyItMatters: These commands act at once, so predicting their arguments is how you avoid deleting or overwriting the wrong thing.

recap.keyIdea: The shell expands patterns and splits words before a command runs, so you can predict what a file command will do by working out the arguments it receives.

blocks.text: A star, a question mark or a bracket set in a word is replaced by the matching names before the program starts, and a pattern that matches nothing is passed on unchanged. Blanks separate words and quotes keep them together, which is why touch my file makes two files and touch "my file" makes one.
Since rm removes at once and mv replaces an existing target without asking, check what a pattern matches with ls first, and use -i where a target might already exist.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks under the names: what a file name actually is, how two names can reach one file, and how a second disk appears in the tree.

lessons.title: Links, inodes and mounts

steps.headline: A directory is a table of names, each pointing at an inode, and the inode is what holds the file's details and its data.

lead.text: When you list a directory, the names you see are not the file. A directory is a table with two columns, a name and a number, and the number identifies an **inode**, the record on the disk that holds the file's size, owner, permissions and times, and says where its data is stored. A name in a directory is an entry that points at an inode, and the inode has no name of its own. The command ls -i shows the numbers.

This separation explains several things that would otherwise seem odd. Renaming a file inside a directory, with mv, changes one entry in the table and leaves the inode alone, which is why it is fast even for a huge file. It also means one inode can be reached by more than one name, and the first view of the figure shows an ordinary file, with the second showing a file that has two names and the third a different kind of pointer.

afterFigure.text: The tags and the inode boxes in the figure are only a picture, and the inode number 1204 is invented as an example. On a real system ls -i prints a number like it beside each name.

diagram.alt: Directory entries drawn as name tags tied to an inode box on the disk. With one name, ha points at an inode. After ln ha hb, two names point at the same inode, and the link count is 2. A symbolic link hc points at a separate inode that stores the path hb.
diagram.caption: Names and inodes. Use the buttons to compare one name, two names for one file, and a symbolic link.

reveal.text: The next screen explains that ln makes a second name and that the second field of ls -l counts the names.

steps.headline: A hard link is a second name for the same inode, and the data survives until the last name is removed.

lead.text: The command ln, with two names, makes a **hard link**: ln ha hb adds the name hb to the directory, pointing at the inode that ha already points at. The second field of ls -l, the link count we skipped before, is the number of names an inode has, so after ln both ha and hb show 2. Neither is the original, since both are equally names for the file, and a change made through either name is a change to the one file.

Removing is then a matter of counting. rm ha removes the name ha and lowers the count from 2 to 1, and the data is untouched because hb still points at it. Only when the last name is removed, and the count reaches zero, does the system free the space. This is why rm a does not always delete the data: the data belongs to the inode, and rm removes only a name.

afterFigure.text: A hard link has two limits. It can only point at a file on the same disk, because inode numbers are local to one disk, and the system does not allow one to a directory.

diagram.alt: Three stages of a file with two hard-linked names, ha and hb. After ln the inode has a link count of 2. After rm ha the count is 1 and hb still reaches the data. After rm hb the count is 0 and the space is freed.
diagram.caption: Removing a name lowers the link count. The data goes only when the count reaches zero. Step through the three views.

reveal.text: Each ln adds one name, so the count is the number of names the file has at that moment.

steps.headline: A symbolic link is a small file that stores a path, so it breaks if the target is removed.

lead.text: There is a second kind of link, made with ln -s. A **symbolic link** is a file in its own right, with its own inode, and the only thing it holds is a path: ln -s hb hc makes hc a file that says hb. Listed with ls -l it shows type l, and an arrow, as in hc -> hb. When a program opens hc, the system reads the stored path and opens that name instead.

Because it follows a name and not an inode, a symbolic link behaves differently from a hard link. It can point at a directory or at a file on another disk. It is not a copy, and it does not count as a name for the target, so rm hb leaves the data gone and hc still listed but unusable: cat hc fails with No such file or directory. A link in this state is called **dangling**. The figure shows the same link before and after the target is removed.

afterFigure.text: That makes the choice simple. Use a hard link to keep a file alive under two names on the same disk, and a symbolic link to point at a place that might be anywhere, accepting that the pointer can break.

diagram.alt: A symbolic link hc stores the path hb. While the name hb exists, cat hc follows the path to the data. After rm hb the stored path leads nowhere and cat hc fails with No such file or directory, so hc is a dangling link.
diagram.caption: A symbolic link follows a name, not the data. Use the buttons to remove the target.

reveal.text: A dangling link still shows up in ls -l with type l, so you find it by trying to open it, and not by looking at the listing.

steps.headline: Follow touch ha; ln ha hb; rm ha; cat hb, then ln -s hb hc; rm hb; cat hc, and say what each leaves.

workedSteps.text: touch makes one name, ha, pointing at one inode.
ln ha hb adds a second name for the same inode. How many inodes does the file have now?
rm ha removes one name. hb remains, so cat hb still prints the data.
ln -s hb hc makes a new small file that stores the path hb.
rm hb removes the last name of the data, so the data is freed and hc stores a path that leads nowhere.
cat hc now fails with No such file or directory, and hc is a dangling link.

steps.headline: Find the link count of hb after echo hi > ha; ln ha hb; rm ha.

workedSteps.text: echo hi > ha makes the file ha, with one name.
ln ha hb adds a name, so the count rises to 2.
rm ha removes one name. Work out the count ls -l shows for hb.

steps.headline: A second disk is attached to a directory called a mount point, and its files appear in the one tree from there.

lead.text: Everything so far happened inside a single tree, and the same is true when you plug in a second disk. Each disk or partition holds a filesystem of its own, with its own inodes. To use it, the system **mounts** it on an empty directory, the **mount point**, and from that moment the files of the new filesystem appear below that directory. A stick mounted at /mnt/usb makes its top level appear as /mnt/usb, and a file photo.jpg on it becomes /mnt/usb/photo.jpg, in the same tree as everything else.

The command df shows the filesystems that are mounted and where. The tree can also hold filesystems that have no disk at all: /proc, met earlier, is made up by the kernel to describe the running system, and /dev holds a name for each device. Since a filesystem has its own inode numbers, a hard link cannot cross from one to another, which is the limit mentioned above.

lessons.orientation: Explain what a file name is, how hard and symbolic links differ, and how a second disk appears in the one tree.
lessons.nextAction: Predict where a command's output goes when it is redirected or piped, and tell standard output from standard error.

blocks.text: Run ls -i in a directory and every name has a number beside it, such as 1204 beside report.txt. The number identifies an inode, the record on the disk that holds the file's size, owner, permissions and times and says where its data is stored, and the name you see is only an entry in the directory that points at that record.

That split decides what the commands for removing and linking really do. rm removes a name and not the record, so the data goes only when no name points at it any more, and a link is either a second name for the same record or a small file that stores a path and stops working when that path no longer leads anywhere. A second disk joins the same tree in a similar way, by being attached to a directory, so its files appear under an ordinary path.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to count the names a file has, predict what happens to a symbolic link when its target is removed, and give the path of a file on a mounted disk.
intro.whyItMatters: Knowing what rm removes tells you whether data is really gone, and links are how one file shows up in several places.

recap.keyIdea: A name is an entry that points at an inode, so a file can have several names, and a second disk joins the same tree at a mount point.

blocks.text: A hard link adds a name for the same inode and raises the link count, and the data is freed only when the count reaches zero. A symbolic link is a separate small file that stores a path, so it can cross disks and point at directories, but it dangles if the target is removed.
A filesystem on another disk is mounted on a directory, and its files appear below it, so there are no drive letters and the tree stays single.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at what programs do with text, where it comes from and where it goes: the three streams and the pipes that join commands.

lessons.title: Streams, redirection and pipes

steps.headline: Every program starts with three streams, one for input, one for output and one for errors, and the shell decides where each one leads.

lead.text: Run ls and its listing appears in the terminal, which makes it look as if the program wrote to the screen. It did not. Every program starts with three **streams**, numbered ones it reads from or writes to: **standard input**, number 0, which is the keyboard by default, **standard output**, number 1, and **standard error**, number 2. Output and errors are both shown in the terminal unless you say otherwise, and that is why they seem to be one thing.

The program neither knows nor cares what its streams are connected to. Before it starts, the shell decides where each leads, and a stream can end up in a file, in another program or in nothing. The figure shows the first view, in which both output streams reach the terminal, and then two ways of changing the destination of stream 1 only.

afterFigure.text: Splitting errors from output is deliberate. A program that prints results and complaints on the same stream would make its results impossible to use in a pipeline, and the next screens show how the split lets you keep one and look at the other.

diagram.alt: A program box with three streams. Stream 0 is input from the keyboard, stream 1 is output and stream 2 is error. In the first view both output streams go to the terminal. With > out.txt only stream 1 goes to a file. With a pipe only stream 1 goes to the next program.
diagram.caption: Three streams leave every program. Use the buttons to see where each goes.

reveal.text: The next screen names the operators and says which stream each one redirects.

steps.headline: The operator > sends standard output to a file and empties it first, >> appends, < feeds a file to standard input, and 2> redirects standard error.

lead.text: **Redirection** changes where a stream leads. The operator > sends standard output to a file, creating the file or **emptying it first** if it exists. That is a destructive step of the kind we met earlier, since echo b > f replaces whatever f held. The operator >> sends standard output to the end of the file and keeps what was there. The operator < goes the other way and feeds a file to standard input, so wc -l < notes.txt reads notes.txt without being given its name.

Each of these acts on one stream only, and a number in front chooses it: 2> sends standard error to a file, and 2>/dev/null sends it to a special file that discards everything written to it. Without a number the operator means stream 1, which is why > leaves error messages on the terminal. With these four, a command's results and its complaints can be kept apart.

reveal.text: The single > empties the file before writing, so only the final command's output remains.

steps.headline: A pipe connects the output of one program to the input of the next, and both programs run at the same time.

lead.text: A **pipe**, written |, connects standard output of the command on its left to standard input of the command on its right, with no file in between. What flows through it is bytes, and the two programs run at the same time: the second reads text as the first writes it, and when the first finishes and closes the pipe the second sees the end of its input and finishes too. The second program does not wait for the first to complete.

This is why small programs combine so well. The idea of joining programs like lengths of garden hose was proposed by Doug McIlroy in a 1964 memo, and pipes entered Unix in 1973. In the figure a producer and a consumer are joined by a pipe, and the three views show the start, the bytes in flight and the end.

afterFigure.text: Only standard output enters a pipe. Standard error is left attached to the terminal unless you redirect it, and the next screens look at exactly that.

diagram.alt: A producer program and a consumer program joined by a pipe. First both are running, then chunks of output pass through the pipe while the producer is still writing, and finally the producer closes the pipe and the consumer sees the end of its input.
diagram.caption: A pipe carries bytes between two programs that run at the same time. Step through three moments.

reveal.text: The next screen shows how 2>&1 and 2>/dev/null change which lines enter the pipe.

steps.headline: 2>&1 sends standard error to wherever standard output goes, and the order of redirections matters.

lead.text: To make errors travel with the output, write 2>&1. It means that stream 2 is to go where stream 1 is going at that moment, so in G 2>&1 | wc -l the error line joins the pipe, and wc counts all three lines. To remove the errors instead, write 2>/dev/null, and wc counts only the two lines sent to standard output.

The words *at that moment* matter, because redirections are applied from left to right. In ls nosuchfile > out.txt 2>&1 the output goes to the file first, and then the error follows it there, so the message is in out.txt. Reverse them, as in ls nosuchfile 2>&1 > out.txt, and the error is pointed at the terminal, which stream 1 is still using, before stream 1 moves to the file, so the message stays on the terminal and out.txt is empty.

afterFigure.text: Remember it as a copy of a destination, taken at the point where the 2>&1 is read. Anything written after it to stream 1 does not change where stream 2 already goes.

diagram.alt: The same group of commands, G, which prints a, then b to the error stream, then c. Piped with no change, wc counts two lines and b reaches the terminal. With 2>&1 the error stream joins the pipe and wc counts three lines. With 2>/dev/null the error stream is discarded and wc counts two.

steps.headline: Count the lines in G 2>&1 | wc -l, where G prints a, then b to standard error, then c.

workedSteps.text: G writes a to standard output, b to standard error and c to standard output.
2>&1 points standard error at the place standard output goes, which is the pipe. How many of G's output streams flow into the pipe now?
wc -l receives a, b and c, each ending in a newline.
So the command prints 3, and nothing is left on the terminal.

steps.headline: Count the lines in G 2>&1 >/dev/null | wc -l, with the same group G.

workedSteps.text: 2>&1 comes first, so standard error is pointed at the pipe, which is where standard output goes at that moment.
The next redirection, >/dev/null, moves standard output only, and the pipe keeps standard error.
Work out how many lines reach wc.

steps.headline: Each program does one job on a stream of text, and pipes let you combine them into jobs nobody wrote a program for.

lead.text: A program that only reads standard input and writes standard output is called a **filter**, and most of the commands you will meet in the next lessons are filters: grep selects lines, sort orders them, wc counts them. None of them knows about the others, and none needs to, since the pipe between them is made by the shell.

The result is a way of working in which a new job is rarely a new program. To find out how many users have a login shell, you do not write code: you select lines, pick a field and count, with three filters joined by two pipes. The rest of this module is mostly about learning those filters.

reveal.text: The error message is one line, and it is now in the file along with whatever the program printed to standard output, which was nothing.

lessons.orientation: Predict where a command's output goes when it is redirected or piped, and distinguish standard output from standard error.
lessons.nextAction: Choose between grep for contents and find for names and attributes, and predict their counts on a small fixed example.

blocks.text: The line ls /etc | wc -l prints one number, the count of the entries in /etc, although ls only lists names and wc only counts lines. The | hands everything ls writes to wc as its input, and wc -l counts the lines it receives. Each program reads text and writes text, and the shell chooses what those texts are connected to, which here is the other program.

Because the shell decides where a program's text goes, the same command can write to the terminal, to a file or into another command without being changed, and a program keeps a separate stream for its complaints so that they need not mix with its results. Seeing where each stream goes is what lets you say what a longer line will leave in a file or hand to the next command.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say where each stream of a command goes, and how many lines a redirection or pipeline leaves in a file or reaches the next program.
intro.whyItMatters: Almost everything you do later is a pipeline, and a pipeline is only as reliable as your picture of where its streams go.

recap.keyIdea: Every program has an input, an output and an error stream, and the shell decides where each leads, so a command's behaviour depends on its redirections as well as its words.

blocks.text: The operator > sends standard output to a file and empties it first, >> appends, < reads a file as input and 2> redirects errors. A pipe connects one program's standard output to the next program's input, with both running at the same time, and it carries only standard output.
2>&1 sends errors wherever output is going at that point, and redirections are applied from left to right, so the order in which you write them changes the result.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson uses these pipes to search: grep for the lines of a file that match, and find for the files that match.

lessons.title: Searching with grep and find

steps.headline: grep prints the lines of a file that contain a pattern, and a pattern is a piece of text, not a field.

lead.text: Suppose a web server writes one line to a log for every request, as access.log does here: the address that asked, the method, the page, and a three-digit status. A file of this kind soon holds thousands of lines, and the usual job is to pick out the few that matter. The command for that is grep, used as grep 404 access.log, which prints each line of the file that contains the text 404.

The pattern is an ordinary piece of text that is looked for anywhere in a line, and grep knows nothing of the columns. That has a consequence that the figure makes plain. The pattern 404 selects one line, 200 selects four, and the pattern 0 selects all six, because every address contains a zero, whether or not anyone meant the status. A plain pattern is matched against the whole line.

reveal.text: The next screen names the options that change what grep prints, and -c is the one that counts.

steps.headline: The options -c, -v, -n and -i change what grep prints, and -c counts matching lines.

lead.text: Four options cover most uses. With -c grep prints only the number of lines that match, and not the lines themselves. With -v it prints the lines that do *not* match, so grep -v 200 access.log prints the two lines whose status is not 200. With -n it puts the line number and a colon in front of each match, as in 2:beta, and with -i it ignores the difference between capital and small letters. The option -r searches every file under a directory instead of one file.

-c counts lines and not matches. A line that holds the pattern twice still counts once, and that matters whenever you read a count as a number of events. grep also reports its result in its **exit status**, the number a command leaves behind for the shell: 0 when it found a match, 1 when it found none, and 2 when something went wrong, such as a missing file.

afterFigure.text: The exit status is how a script can ask whether a pattern is present without printing anything, which is a use that the lesson on scripts returns to.

reveal.text: The count follows the addresses, since no other field holds the digit. A pattern is matched wherever its text appears.
The next screen explains what find prints, and in particular what it does with the starting point.

steps.headline: find walks a directory tree and tests each entry by name, type, size or age, and the starting directory is itself an entry.

lead.text: grep looks inside files, while **find** looks at the files themselves. It is given a starting directory and walks down through everything beneath it, and each entry it meets is tested. The test -name '*.log' keeps entries whose names match the pattern, -type d keeps directories and -type f keeps ordinary files, and others such as -size and -mtime test the size and the age. With no test at all find prints every entry.

Two details cause most of the mistakes. The starting directory is an entry like any other, so find . -type d includes the dot in its count, and in the tree of the figure it prints three directories, not two. And the pattern after -name must be quoted, as in -name '*.log', so that the shell leaves the star alone and find does the matching itself, in every subdirectory. Unquoted, the shell would expand the star against the current directory first, as an earlier lesson showed.

steps.headline: Work out how many lines grep -v 200 access.log | wc -l prints.

workedSteps.text: The pipe hands the output of grep -v 200 to wc -l, which counts lines. First work out how many lines hold the text 200.
-v prints the lines that do not match, so the other lines of the six are the ones printed.
wc -l counts those two lines.

steps.headline: Work out how many lines find . -name '*.log' | wc -l prints in a tree holding a/x.log, a/b/y.log and z.txt.

workedSteps.text: find walks down from the dot and tests the name of every entry it meets.
Only the names that end in .log pass the test.
wc -l counts the lines find printed. Write the number.

steps.headline: Use grep to choose lines by their text and find to choose files by their attributes, and join them when you need both.

lead.text: The two commands answer different questions. grep answers *what is inside*, find answers *which files exist*, and the figure sets out the choice. When you need both, find can produce the names and a pipe can hand them on: find . -name '*.log' | xargs grep -l ERROR prints the names of the log files that contain the word ERROR, where xargs turns the names it reads into arguments for grep and -l asks grep to list file names rather than lines.

The shorter form grep -r ERROR . does the same search without a pipe when no test on the name is needed. Neither form is better in general, but find lets you restrict by name, size or age before any text is read, which is cheaper on a large tree.

diagram.alt: Two cards. The first says that grep answers what is inside the files, for example grep -r ERROR /var/log. The second says that find answers which files exist, by name, type, size or age, for example find /var/log -name '*.log'.

reveal.text: The number comes from the file and not from the count of matches, so it stays the same if other lines are removed from the output.
Reading the status lets a script act on a search without printing the matches, which a later lesson uses.
The option -w would restrict the match to whole words and so leave the new line out, which is the usual remedy.

lessons.orientation: Choose between grep for contents and find for names and attributes, and predict their counts on a small fixed example.
lessons.nextAction: Read and write small regular expressions using anchors, character classes, repetition and alternation.

blocks.text: The command grep ERROR app.log prints each line of app.log that contains the text ERROR, and find . -name '*.log' prints the path of every file below the current directory whose name ends in .log, however deeply it is nested. Between them they reduce a tree of files holding thousands of lines to the few lines that matter.

grep answers what is inside a file and find answers which files exist, and each prints plain lines of text that wc or another filter can count. A search with a slightly wrong pattern still prints something, so the way to check one is to work out how many lines it should print and compare that with what it does print.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say how many lines grep or find will print on a small fixed example, and when to choose each.
intro.whyItMatters: Counting what a search prints is how you check a command before you trust it.

recap.keyIdea: grep chooses lines by the text they contain and find chooses files by their names and attributes, and both can be checked by counting what they print.

blocks.text: grep prints the lines that match a pattern, -c counts them, -v inverts the match, -n numbers them, and a plain pattern matches wherever its text appears, so 0 matches every line in a log whose addresses contain a zero. It exits with 0 when it found a match, 1 when it found none and 2 on an error.

find walks a tree from a starting directory and tests each entry, including the starting directory itself, so find . -type d counts the dot. Quote the pattern given to -name so that find, not the shell, does the matching.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson says more exactly what a pattern can describe: where in a line a match must be, which characters it allows and how many times they may repeat.

lessons.title: Regular expressions

steps.headline: A regular expression describes a set of strings, with literal characters, a dot for any one character, and classes for one character from a set.

lead.text: Plain text is already a pattern: cat describes the strings that contain the three letters c, a and t in a row. A **regular expression**, or **regex**, adds operators that let one pattern describe many strings. The simplest is the dot, which stands for any one character, so a.c describes a, then any single character, then c. It matches abc, axc and a.c, but not ac, in which nothing stands between a and c, and not axxc, in which two characters do.

A **character class** in square brackets names the characters that may appear in one position: [a-z] is any one small letter, [0-9] any one digit, and [57] either a 5 or a 7. A caret at the start of the class, as in [^0-9], reverses it to any one character that is not a digit. Because the dot is an operator, a real dot has to be written \., with a backslash in front, and the figure shows both patterns on the same four strings.

afterFigure.text: The backslash is the general way of turning an operator back into a plain character. It is easy to forget, since an unescaped dot usually matches the real dot as well, and the mistake only shows when some other character turns up in its place.

diagram.alt: Four strings, abc, a.c, ac and axxc, tested against two patterns. The pattern a.c matches abc and a.c, because the dot stands for any single character. The pattern a\.c matches only a.c, because the backslash makes the dot an ordinary dot.

reveal.text: Only the string with a real dot between the two letters satisfies it, whereas the unescaped dot also admitted other characters.
The next two screens explain repetition and then the anchors, and the figures use the same idea on other strings.

steps.headline: The operators *, + and ? say how many times the previous item may repeat, and the extended syntax of grep -E makes them available.

lead.text: After an item, an operator says how often it may occur. A star * allows any number of repeats, including none, a plus + requires at least one, and a question mark ? allows at most one. So ab*c describes an a, then any number of b, then a c, which matches ac, abc and abbc, while ab+c needs at least one b and rejects ac. A number in braces, as in [0-9]{3}, asks for an exact count, here three digits in a row.

The star differs from the star of a glob, which stands for any characters. In a regular expression it repeats the item before it, so *.txt does not mean what it means to the shell. These operators belong to the **extended** syntax, which you select with grep -E. In the basic syntax that grep uses by default the characters + ? | ( ) { } are plain characters unless escaped, and this course uses -E throughout.

steps.headline: A caret anchors a pattern to the start of a line and a dollar sign to its end, so a pattern with both must match the whole line.

lead.text: Without anchors a pattern may match anywhere in a line, so cat matches the line cat, but also cat5, cats and concatenate. An **anchor** ties it down: ^ matches the start of the line and $ the end. The pattern ^cat$ then matches only a line that is exactly cat, and ^[a-z]+$ matches only a line made of one or more small letters from its first character to its last.

The last pattern shows why the anchors matter. Of the five lines cat, Cat, cat5, an empty line and cats, it matches cat and cats. Cat fails because a capital is outside the class, cat5 because of the digit, and the empty line because the plus needs at least one letter. Take the anchors away and cat5 would match as well, since it contains small letters somewhere.

afterFigure.text: Forgetting the anchors is the commonest error in practice, because a pattern that is loose enough to match what you meant also matches things you did not.

steps.headline: Count the lines that grep -Ec '^[a-z]+$' selects from cat, Cat, cat5, an empty line and cats.

workedSteps.text: The pattern describes the whole line: one or more small letters and nothing else. The plus requires how many letters at the very least?
cat is three small letters, so it matches.
Cat starts with a capital, which [a-z] does not allow, and cat5 ends in a digit.
The empty line has no letter at all, but the plus needs one. cats is four small letters.
Two lines match, so grep -Ec prints 2.

steps.headline: Count the lines of the six-line log selected by the pattern ^10\.0\.0\.[57] , where 10.0.0.5 starts three lines, 10.0.0.7 two and 10.0.0.9 one.

workedSteps.text: The anchor ties the address to the start of the line, and each escaped dot is a real dot.
The class [57] allows a last digit of 5 or 7, and the space after it ends the address. The lines starting 10.0.0.9 are excluded.
Add the lines of the addresses that the class allows, and write the number.

steps.headline: A bar separates alternatives, and parentheses group them, so one pattern can stand for several words.

lead.text: The last operator is the bar |, which offers a choice: cat|dog matches a line containing either word. Parentheses group part of a pattern so that the bar applies only to that part, as in  (404|302)$, which matches a line that ends in either status. Without the parentheses, 404|302$ would mean 404 anywhere, or 302 at the end, because the bar divides the whole pattern.

With this you can read most patterns you will meet: literal text, a dot or class for one character, an operator for how often, anchors for where, and the bar for which. The notation comes from the mathematician Stephen Kleene, who described *regular events* in 1951, and Ken Thompson built it into the QED editor in the 1960s, from which it reached grep. The name grep itself is a command in the editor ed: g/re/p, which prints the lines matching a regular expression.

reveal.text: Extended syntax is the form this course uses, so you will see -E before most patterns that use these operators.
The group keeps the bar from dividing the whole pattern, and the anchor keeps the match to the end of the line.

lessons.orientation: Read and write a small regular expression using anchors, character classes, repetition and alternation, and say which strings it matches.
lessons.nextAction: Build a pipeline of sort, uniq, cut, tr, sed and awk that turns a log or a table into a count or a summary.

blocks.text: The pattern ^[a-z]+$ selects the lines of a file that consist of nothing but small letters. The caret stands for the start of the line, the brackets list the characters allowed, here the letters a to z, the plus lets that choice repeat as often as it likes provided it occurs at least once, and the dollar sign stands for the end of the line. A line such as hello satisfies all four, and a line such as hello! does not, because the exclamation mark is neither a small letter nor the end of the line.

A pattern of this kind is called a regular expression, and the notation is read in the same way wherever you meet it, in grep, in the editors, in sed and awk and in most programming languages. Its symbols look like those of the glob patterns you used for file names but mean different things: a star in a glob stands for any characters, whereas a star in a regular expression repeats the item before it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say which strings a small regular expression matches, and to write one with anchors, classes, repetition and alternation.
intro.whyItMatters: A precise pattern selects what you meant and nothing else, so you can trust a count taken with it.

recap.keyIdea: A regular expression describes a set of strings with literals, a dot or class for one character, repetition operators, anchors and alternation, and an unanchored pattern matches anywhere in a line.

blocks.text: The dot stands for any one character and a class in brackets for one character from a set. The operators * + ? and {n} say how many times the previous item repeats, and ^ and $ anchor a pattern to the start and end of a line, so that ^[a-z]+$ must match the whole line.
A bar with parentheses offers alternatives, and a backslash turns an operator back into a plain character, so a\.c matches only a.c. In grep these operators need the option -E.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson takes the output of grep and the other filters further: sorting it, counting it, cutting fields from it and editing it.

lessons.title: Transforming text

steps.headline: A line splits into fields at a delimiter, and cut or awk takes the one you want.

lead.text: A log or a table is a list of records, and each record holds several values in a fixed order. The six lines of access.log each hold an address, a method, a page and a status, separated by single blanks. Each value is a **field**, and the blank that separates them is the **delimiter**. To take one field from every line, cut uses -d for the delimiter and -f for the field number, as in cut -d' ' -f4, and awk numbers its fields from $1 and splits at blanks by default, so awk '{print $4}' prints the same column.

The figure highlights one column at a time. Field 1 is the address, which is the one to count if you want to know who is asking, and field 4 is the status, which tells you whether the request worked. Most of what follows is a short chain of commands that starts from one of these columns.

afterFigure.text: Both tools can change the separator: cut -d, uses a comma and awk -F, does the same, which is what a comma-separated table needs.

The next screen explains how sort compares lines, and what changes with -n.

steps.headline: sort orders lines as text by default, so 300 comes before 40, and sort -n orders them as numbers.

lead.text: sort puts the lines of its input in order, but the order it uses by default is the order of characters, as in a dictionary. It compares the first characters of two lines, and moves on to the next only if they tie. So 100 comes before 9 because 1 comes before 9, and 300 comes before 40 because 3 comes before 4, however much larger the numbers are. When the values are numbers, -n compares them as numbers instead, and the order becomes 9, 10, 100.

Two other options are used constantly. -r reverses the order, so sort -rn puts the largest number first, and -u keeps only one copy of each distinct line. A forgotten -n is one of the commonest reasons for a sorted list of numbers that looks wrong.

afterFigure.text: The figure sorts the same three lines both ways. Since the output is the same text in a different order, nothing but the comparison has changed.

diagram.alt: The numbers 10, 9 and 100 sorted two ways. Sorted as text they come out as 10, 100, 9. Sorted with -n as numbers they come out as 9, 10, 100.
