reveal.text: The next screen explains what uniq compares, and how the pair sort and uniq counts how often each value occurs.

steps.headline: uniq collapses neighbouring equal lines, so sort | uniq -c | sort -rn counts how often each value occurs and ranks them.

lead.text: uniq compares each line with the one just before it, and collapses a run of equal lines into one. It does not look further back, so two equal lines that are not neighbours both survive. Its input must therefore be sorted first, which puts equal lines together. With the option -c, uniq puts the length of each run in front of the line, and so produces a count.

That gives the standard recipe for counting values. Take one column, sort it, count the runs with uniq -c, and sort the counts with sort -rn to put the biggest first. Applied to the addresses of access.log, awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -1 prints 3 10.0.0.5, so that address made three of the six requests. The figure shows the text after each stage.

afterFigure.text: head -1 keeps only the first line, which here is the most frequent value. Remove it and you get the whole ranking.

diagram.alt: The six addresses of access.log passing through four stages of a pipeline. First one address per line, then sorted so equal addresses are neighbours, then counted with uniq -c as 3 for 10.0.0.5, 2 for 10.0.0.7 and 1 for 10.0.0.9, then sorted by count with the biggest first.

reveal.text: After sort the two copies of each line are neighbours, and uniq can collapse them.

steps.headline: sed replaces text in a stream and tr replaces single characters, and neither changes the original file.

lead.text: Sometimes the text itself has to change. The command sed edits a stream line by line, and its commonest command is a substitution, s/old/new/, which replaces the first match of old on each line with new. In echo aXbXc | sed 's/X/-/' the output is a-bXc, since only the first X on the line is replaced. With the flag g at the end, s/X/-/g, every match on the line is replaced and the output is a-b-c. The old text is a regular expression of the kind the last lesson covered.

sed prints the changed text and leaves the file alone, so sed 's/x/y/' f shows what f would look like, and f is unchanged afterwards. The option -i edits the file in place, and it is worth running without it first. tr works on single characters rather than patterns: tr a-z A-Z turns small letters into capitals, and tr ' ' '\n' turns each blank into a newline, which splits a line into one word per line.

steps.headline: awk reads lines, splits them into fields and runs a small program of pattern and action pairs, with END running once at the end.

lead.text: awk is a small programming language built for records. A program is a list of pairs, each a pattern and an action in braces, as in $4==200 {print $1}, which prints the address of every line whose status is 200. A pair without a pattern runs on every line, and END { ... } runs once after the last line has been read. Variables start at zero, so awk -F, '{s+=$2} END{print s}' adds the second field of every line to s and prints the sum at the end.

That is enough to total a column, count the lines that satisfy a test, or print selected fields in a new order. The commands in this lesson can do the same jobs in many ways, so the choice between them is partly habit: cut for one field, sort and uniq for counting, sed for editing text, and awk when you need arithmetic or a condition.

steps.headline: Work out what awk -F, '{s+=$2} END{print s}' prints for the lines dee,2 and ev,6 and fay,1.

workedSteps.text: -F, splits each line at the comma, so $2 is the number after the name. Before any line is read, s holds nothing, which counts as zero.
The first line adds its field 2 to s, and the second adds its own. What does s hold after the second line?
The third line adds 1.
END runs once, after the last line, and prints the total.

steps.headline: Work out how many dashes echo 'aXbXc' | sed 's/X/-/' prints.

workedSteps.text: The line aXbXc has two X characters, and the substitution is s/X/-/.
There is no g flag, so sed replaces only the first match on the line.
Count the dashes in the output and write the number.

reveal.text: Dropping the counts gives the number of different values, which is a different question from which value is most common.

lessons.orientation: Build a pipeline of sort, uniq, cut, tr, sed and awk that turns a log or a table into a count or a summary.
lessons.nextAction: Read and write permission modes in symbolic and octal form, and predict what a user may do to a file or a directory.

blocks.text: The line awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -1 reads a web log and prints the address that made the most requests, a job that no single command does. It takes the first field of every line, puts equal addresses side by side, counts each run and keeps the run with the biggest count, and each of those steps is a separate small program that sees only the text handed to it.

Each command does one thing to text and the pipe hands the result to the next, so a job nobody wrote a program for is built by choosing small commands and putting them in the right order. A pipeline gives the answer you meant only if you know what each stage does to the text it receives, and you can work that out on a few lines before you run it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to predict what a pipeline of sort, uniq, cut, tr, sed and awk prints on a small fixed input.
intro.whyItMatters: Counting and summarising text from the command line is the quickest way to answer a question about a log or a table.

recap.keyIdea: A pipeline of small text commands turns a log or a table into a count or a summary, and each command's behaviour can be predicted on a fixed example.

blocks.text: cut and awk take a field from every line, sort orders lines as text unless -n makes it numeric, and uniq collapses only neighbouring equal lines, so sort | uniq -c | sort -rn counts and ranks the values of a column. sed s/old/new/ replaces the first match on each line, g replaces them all, and neither changes the file unless -i is used.
awk runs a pattern and action on each line, keeps variables that start at zero, and runs END once at the end, which makes it the tool for totals.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns from the contents of files to who may use them: permissions, ownership and the octal numbers that write them down.

lessons.title: Permissions and ownership

steps.headline: A file's mode is nine bits, read, write and execute for its owner, for its group and for everyone else.

lead.text: The first column of ls -l ends with nine characters, such as rwxr-xr-- , that record who may do what to the file. They come in three groups of three. The first group applies to the file's **owner**, the second to its **group**, and the third to **others**, meaning everyone else. In each group the three characters are, in order, **read** (r), **write** (w) and **execute** (x), and a dash in a place means that the bit is off.

For a file, read allows its contents to be read, write allows them to be changed, and execute allows the file to be run as a program. The nine bits taken together are called the file's **mode**. The figure shows three common modes, with the digits beneath them that the next screen explains.

afterFigure.text: The kernel checks these bits every time a process opens a file, so they are not advice. A process that lacks a bit is refused, whatever the program intended.

diagram.alt: Nine permission bits as three groups of three boxes for owner, group and others, with the octal digit of each group beneath. Three modes are shown: rwxr-xr--, rw-r----- and rw-r--r--.

reveal.text: The next screen explains how each group of bits becomes one octal digit, so a mode is a three-digit number.

steps.headline: Each group of three bits is one octal digit, found by adding 4 for read, 2 for write and 1 for execute.

lead.text: It is shorter to write a mode as a number than as nine characters, and the conversion is mechanical. Give read the value 4, write the value 2 and execute the value 1, and add the values of the bits that are on in a group. The group rwx is 4 + 2 + 1, which is 7, the group r-x is 4 + 0 + 1, which is 5, and the group r-- is 4 alone. Written side by side the three digits make **754**, an **octal** number, one whose digits run from 0 to 7.

The digits are not added together, since each one stands for a separate group. Read it backwards when you need the string: the digit 6 is 4 + 2, so read and write, which is rw-, and the digit 0 is no bits at all. Mode 640 is therefore rw- for the owner, r-- for the group and --- for others, written rw-r-----.

afterFigure.text: The same value 7 means all three bits whichever group it stands in, so you only have to learn eight digits.

diagram.alt: The mode rwxr-xr-- with one group of bits highlighted at a time. The owner group rwx is 4 + 2 + 1, which is 7. The group part r-x is 4 + 0 + 1, which is 5. The others part r-- is 4 + 0 + 0, which is 4.

reveal.text: The conversion works in both directions, and you will do it often when you read other people's file listings.

steps.headline: chmod changes a mode, either by naming the new digits or by naming the bits to change.

lead.text: The command chmod sets the mode of a file. In its octal form you give the new digits, so chmod 640 notes.txt sets exactly that mode and replaces whatever was there. In its symbolic form you name who, an operator and the bits: u stands for the owner, g for the group, o for others and a for all three, + switches bits on, - switches them off and = sets them exactly. So chmod u+x notes.txt adds the execute bit for the owner and leaves every other bit alone, and chmod g+w,o-r changes two groups at once.

The two forms suit different jobs. The octal form is exact and short when you know the whole mode you want. The symbolic form is the safer choice when you want to change one thing, since it cannot disturb the bits you did not name. A file with mode 644 becomes 744 after chmod u+x.

reveal.text: The digits you did not name keep their values, which is the advantage of the symbolic form.
The next screen explains what each of the three bits means for a directory, which is different from their meaning for a file.

steps.headline: On a directory, read lists the names, write creates and removes entries, and execute lets you pass through to what is inside.

lead.text: The same nine bits mean something different on a directory, which is a list of names. **Read** lets you list the names it holds. **Write** lets you change the list, so you can create, rename or remove entries in it. **Execute**, which is better thought of as search, lets you pass through the directory to reach a name inside it, so without it you cannot open a file in the directory even if you know the file's name and may read it.

That is why removing a file is governed by the directory. A file's name is an entry in its directory, so rm changes the directory, and what it needs is write permission there. The bits of the file itself decide who may read or change its contents, and have no say in whether its name can be removed. The figure shows what three people may do in one directory.

diagram.alt: A directory d with mode rwxr-x---, owned by ana and group staff. Three views show what each of three people can do in it. The owner ana can list names, create or remove entries and enter. The group member bo can list names and enter but not create or remove entries. Anyone else, cy, can do none of the three.

steps.headline: The first matching group decides, and the umask removes bits from the mode that a new file starts with.

lead.text: Every file has an owner, a user, and a group. When a process asks for access, the kernel picks one triplet: the owner's if the process runs as the owner, otherwise the group's if it runs as a member of the group, and the others' if neither applies. It does not combine them, so an owner can have fewer rights than the group, and the user **root** can read and write nearly everything. chown changes the owner and group of a file, and only root may use it to give a file away.

New files also need a mode. They start from 666 for files and 777 for directories, and the **umask** says which bits to remove. A umask of 027 clears the write bit for the group, from 6 to 4, and every bit for others, from 6 to 0, so a new file gets 640 and a new directory 750. The removal is bit by bit and not by subtracting whole numbers, although the two agree when the umask clears only bits that are set.

steps.headline: Work out the mode of a new file when the umask is 027.

workedSteps.text: A new file starts from 666, and the umask digits are 0, 2 and 7, one for each group.
The owner digit of the umask is 0, so no bits are removed and the owner keeps 6.
The group digit of the umask is 2, which is the write bit. Removing it from 6 leaves which digit for the group?
The others digit of the umask is 7, which removes every bit, so others get 0.
Written side by side the new file's mode is 640, and a new directory, from 777, gets 750.

steps.headline: Work out the mode of a new file under the common umask 022.

workedSteps.text: The digits of the umask are 0, 2 and 2, and the file starts from 666.
The owner keeps both bits, and the group and others each lose the write bit.
Write the three digits as one number.

reveal.text: The owner's write bit belongs to the owner, and the group member is limited to what the group digit grants.

lessons.orientation: Read and write permission modes in symbolic and octal form and predict what a user may do to a file or directory.
lessons.nextAction: Say how to see, suspend, resume and stop processes, and what the common signals do.

blocks.text: The line -rwxr-x--- 1 ana staff 2048 Mar 3 10:12 backup.sh makes a precise statement about who may do what with the file. The first character says it is an ordinary file, and the nine that follow say that ana may read it, change it and run it, that members of the group staff may read and run it but not change it, and that everyone else may do nothing with it at all.

That is how a system shared by several people, or by several programs running as different users, keeps one from damaging another's files, and the kernel applies it every time a process opens the file. The same nine characters explain many everyday errors, such as Permission denied when you run a script that has no execute bit, because they show you which bit is missing.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to convert a mode between its nine-character and octal forms, say who may do what to a file or a directory, and predict the mode of a new file.
intro.whyItMatters: Permission errors are among the commonest you will meet, and the mode tells you exactly why.

recap.keyIdea: A mode is nine bits, read, write and execute for the owner, the group and others, and it can be written as three octal digits that are sums of 4, 2 and 1.

blocks.text: Each group of bits is one digit, so rwxr-xr-- is 754, and chmod sets a mode either by digits or by naming the bits to change. On a directory, read lists the names, write creates and removes entries, and execute lets you pass through, which is why removing a file needs write permission on its directory.
The kernel applies the first matching triplet, owner then group then others, and the umask removes bits from the starting modes of 666 for files and 777 for directories.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at the programs that run under these permissions: processes, how to see them, and the signals that stop them.

lessons.title: Processes and signals

steps.headline: Every running program is a process with a number, the PID, and a parent process that started it.

lead.text: Each time the shell starts a program, the system creates a **process** to run it, and gives it a number called its **PID**. Every process also has a **parent**, the process that started it, and so the processes of a running system form a tree. At the top is process 1, started by the kernel at boot, which starts the services; a terminal program is started under it, the shell under the terminal, and the commands you run under the shell.

The command ps lists processes. With the right options it shows the PID, the parent's PID, written PPID, and the name of the command. The figure shows five processes as a tree and as the table that ps would print for them, and each PPID in the table is the PID of the process above it in the tree.

afterFigure.text: A process also has a state, such as running or sleeping, and a use of memory and processor time, which top shows live. For a first reading the PID and the PPID are the two columns that matter.

diagram.alt: A process tree with PID 1 at the top, a terminal program with PID 640 below it, a shell with PID 700 below that, and two commands, sleep with PID 812 and ps with PID 815, started by the shell. A second view shows the same processes as the table that ps prints, with PID, parent PID and command.

reveal.text: The next screen describes the foreground and the background, and what wait does.

steps.headline: A foreground program holds the prompt until it ends, a background one does not, and wait pauses the shell until background jobs end.

lead.text: Normally a command runs in the **foreground**: the shell starts it and waits, and the prompt returns only when it ends. Writing & after a command starts it in the **background** instead, and the shell returns to the prompt at once, so sleep 3 & leaves you free to type while the sleep runs. jobs lists the background jobs of the shell, fg brings one to the foreground and bg lets a suspended one carry on in the background.

The command wait makes the shell pause until its background jobs have finished. That is what fixes the order in sleep 1 & echo started; wait; echo done: the shell starts the sleep, prints started at once, waits a second, and prints done. Two keys are worth knowing. Ctrl-C interrupts the foreground program, and Ctrl-Z **suspends** it, which stops it without ending it, so that bg or fg can resume it. A background job is still attached to its terminal, and closing the terminal sends it the hangup signal.

diagram.alt: Two timelines of three seconds. In the first, sleep 3 runs in the foreground, and the shell waits for it with no prompt. In the second, sleep 3 & runs in the background, and the shell is free at once to take further commands.
diagram.caption: Foreground and background. Use the buttons to compare sleep 3 with sleep 3 &.

reveal.text: A suspended program keeps its place and its memory, so fg or bg continues it from exactly where it stopped.

steps.headline: A signal is a short numbered message to a process, and kill sends one, SIGTERM by default.

lead.text: The keys Ctrl-C and Ctrl-Z work by sending a **signal**, a short numbered message that the kernel delivers to a process. Each has a name and a number. **SIGTERM**, number 15, asks a process to finish and is what kill sends when you give it a PID and nothing else. **SIGINT**, number 2, is what Ctrl-C sends. **SIGHUP**, number 1, says the terminal has closed. **SIGKILL**, number 9, ends a process at once.

The difference between them is whether the program gets a say. A program can catch SIGTERM, SIGINT and SIGHUP, which means it runs its own code when one arrives, to save work and exit cleanly, or to ignore it. SIGKILL cannot be caught or ignored: the kernel removes the process without asking. That makes kill -9 the last resort, since the program gets no chance to tidy up, and you send SIGTERM first. killall and pkill send a signal to processes by name, where kill needs a PID.

afterFigure.text: Suspending uses SIGSTOP and SIGTSTP, and resuming SIGCONT. Their numbers differ between processor families, so this course uses the names, whereas 1, 2, 9 and 15 are the same on every Linux system.

diagram.alt: Three signals sent to a program. kill 4321 sends SIGTERM, number 15, which the program may catch and exit from cleanly. kill -9 4321 sends SIGKILL, number 9, which the kernel acts on without asking the program. Ctrl-C sends SIGINT, number 2, which the program may catch.
diagram.caption: Which signals a program can catch. Use the buttons to compare three.

steps.headline: Follow sleep 1 & echo started; wait; echo done, and say what is printed and in what order.

workedSteps.text: The first command ends in &, so the shell starts the sleep in the background and moves on without waiting.
The shell prints started at once. How many background jobs does the next command, wait, have to wait for?
wait pauses the shell for the one second that the sleep takes.
The sleep ends, wait returns, and the last command prints done.

steps.headline: Follow { sleep 1; echo A; } & echo B; wait; echo C, where the braces group two commands that run together in the background.

workedSteps.text: The group is started in the background, so it will print A after one second, and the shell continues.
The shell prints B at once, and then wait pauses it until the group has finished.
The group prints A, then wait returns and C is printed. Say which letter is the second line.

steps.headline: A process ends with an exit status, 0 for success and anything else for failure, and a process ended by a signal reports 128 plus the signal number.

lead.text: When a process ends it returns a small number to its parent, called its **exit status**. By convention 0 means success and any other value means that something failed, and the shell keeps the status of the last command in the variable $?. After false, echo $? prints 1, and after a sleep that completes normally it prints 0. The number is a signal that the program gives to the program that started it, and not an error message.

A process that is ended by a signal has no chance to choose a status, so bash reports 128 plus the signal number. A program ended by SIGTERM shows 143, and one ended by SIGKILL shows 137. The status therefore tells a script or a person not only that a job failed but, often, how it was ended.

reveal.text: The status adds 128 to the number, so a script can tell a job that was killed from one that failed on its own.

lessons.orientation: Explain how to see, suspend, resume and stop processes, and what the common signals do.
lessons.nextAction: Predict what a command sees in its environment and which program the shell runs when a name appears in several places.

blocks.text: Start sleep 100 at a prompt and the prompt does not come back, because the shell is waiting for the command to finish. Press Ctrl-C and it returns at once: the terminal turns your keystroke into a signal, the kernel delivers that signal to the sleep process, and the process ends. Write sleep 100 & instead, and the prompt comes back immediately while the sleep runs on in the background.

A system is always running many programs like this, each with a number that the system uses to keep track of it. Ctrl-C is one message to a running program, and there are others, from a polite request to finish to an order the program cannot refuse, so the one you choose decides whether the program gets a chance to save its work before it ends.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say what order a line with background jobs prints in, and which signal and which number to use to stop a process.
intro.whyItMatters: Knowing which signal to send, and what a process can do with it, is how you stop a program without damaging its work.

recap.keyIdea: Every running program is a process with a PID and a parent, and the shell can run it in the foreground or background, suspend it and send it signals, each of which it either catches or cannot refuse.

blocks.text: ps lists processes with their PID and parent, & starts a command in the background, and wait pauses the shell until its background jobs end. kill sends SIGTERM, number 15, by default, and kill -9 sends SIGKILL, which a program cannot catch, so SIGTERM comes first.
A process returns an exit status when it ends, 0 for success and any other number for failure, kept in $?, and a process ended by a signal reports 128 plus the signal number.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at what a new process inherits from the shell that started it: its environment variables, and the PATH that decides which program a name refers to.

lessons.title: Variables, environment and PATH

steps.headline: A shell variable is a name that holds a text value, set with name=value and read with a dollar sign.

lead.text: A shell can remember values. A **variable** is a name that holds a piece of text, and you set one by writing the name, an equals sign and the value, with no spaces around the sign: greeting=hi. To use the value, write a dollar sign before the name, and the shell replaces $greeting with hi before it runs the command, in the same way that it replaced a glob with file names. After greeting=hi, the line echo $greeting prints hi.

A variable that you set this way belongs to the shell that you set it in, and to nothing else. It is not part of the file system and it is not in the programs that the shell starts. That is a property worth testing before it is explained, since it decides which programs can see what you set.

reveal.text: The next screen explains which variables a child process receives, and how to make them reach it.

steps.headline: A child receives a copy of the exported variables of its parent, called its environment, and nothing ever travels back.

lead.text: Every process has an **environment**, a set of named values that it can read. When the shell starts a program, it gives the program a copy of its own exported variables, and no others. The command export marks a variable for this: after x=5 and export x, a child started with bash -c 'echo [$x]' prints [5], where before the export it printed [].

The copy goes in one direction only. A child that changes x changes its own copy, and the shell's x stays at 5, because the child has no way to reach back into the process that started it. This explains a common surprise, which is that a script cannot change a variable in the shell that ran it. The figure shows the three cases.

afterFigure.text: Some variables are in the environment from the start: HOME holds your home directory and PATH, which the next screens explain, holds the places searched for commands.

diagram.alt: A shell and a child process drawn as two boxes. When x is set in the shell but not exported, the child has no x. After export, the child starts with its own copy of x equal to 5. If the child then changes x to 9, the shell's x is still 5, because a change never travels back up.
diagram.caption: Variables and child processes. Use the buttons to see the three cases.

steps.headline: Single quotes keep a dollar sign literal, double quotes let it expand, and $( ) replaces a command by its output.

lead.text: Quotes decide whether the shell expands a variable. Inside single quotes everything is literal, so echo '$x' prints the two characters $x. Inside double quotes the dollar sign still works, so echo "$x" prints the value, and the double quotes also keep the result as one word, which matters when a value contains blanks. Quote variables in double quotes unless you have a reason not to.

A command can also supply a value. Writing $( ) around a command runs it first and puts its output where the $( ) was: with x=3 and a command echo "$(echo hi)", echo receives the one word hi. The same form stores a result, as in n=$(wc -l < notes.txt), and it works anywhere a word is expected. The figure shows what echo receives in each case.

diagram.alt: Three lines typed after x=3 and what echo receives. With single quotes echo receives the text $x. With double quotes it receives 3. With a command substitution, echo receives the output of the inner command, hi.
diagram.caption: What the shell hands to echo. Use the buttons to compare the three forms.

The next screen explains how the shell finds a program, and why the order of the directories matters.

steps.headline: PATH is a colon-separated list of directories that the shell searches from left to right, and the first match runs.

lead.text: When you type a command name that is not a built-in, the shell has to find a program with that name. It reads the variable **PATH**, a list of directories separated by colons, and looks in each one from left to right for an executable with that name. The first match is the one that runs, and the search stops there, so a program in an earlier directory hides a program of the same name in a later one. which and type tell you what a name will resolve to.

The current directory is not searched unless PATH contains it, and it usually does not, for the good reason that a stray file named ls in a directory you happened to be in would then replace the real one. To run a program that sits in the current directory, give its path, as in ./tool. The figure shows the same two copies of a program under two orders of PATH.

afterFigure.text: For the same reason a script that must behave the same everywhere either uses full paths for its commands, or sets its own PATH at the top.

diagram.alt: A PATH of two directories that both hold a program called tool. With /usr/local/bin first, the copy there runs and the one in /usr/bin is never reached. With /usr/bin first, the copy in /usr/bin runs.
diagram.caption: The directories of PATH are tried from left to right. Use the buttons to reverse their order.

reveal.text: Only the directories listed in PATH are searched, which is why ./tool, with its path, is needed.

steps.headline: Follow name=ana; export name; bash -c 'name=bo; echo $name'; echo $name, and say what is printed.

workedSteps.text: name=ana sets a variable in the shell, and export marks it, so a child receives a copy of it.
The child starts with its own copy and sets that copy to bo. How many separate copies of the variable exist now?
The child prints its own copy, which is bo, and then ends.
The shell prints its own copy, which was never changed.

steps.headline: Work out what n=$(echo hello | wc -c); echo "$n" prints.

workedSteps.text: The shell runs the command inside $( ) first. echo hello prints the five letters and a newline.
wc -c counts the bytes of that text, which are the letters and the newline.
The output replaces the $( ), so n holds a number. Say what echo "$n" prints.

reveal.text: The program that a name refers to depends on the order of PATH, so changing the order changes the program with no change to either file.

lessons.orientation: Predict what a command sees in its environment and which program the shell runs when a name appears in several places.
lessons.nextAction: Read a short shell script and say what it prints and what exit status it returns, using conditions, loops and arguments.

blocks.text: Type echo $HOME and the shell prints the path of your home directory, perhaps /home/ana. HOME is a variable, a name that holds a piece of text, and the shell replaces $HOME with that text before echo runs. PATH is another, and its text is a list of directories separated by colons, which the shell consults to turn a command name such as python into a program on the disk.

A shell keeps variables so that it can remember values, and it decides which of them to hand on to the programs it starts, which is why a command can behave differently in two shells. Knowing which variables a program can see, and which program a name leads to, lets you say what a command will do before you run it, and why one that worked in one place fails in another.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say what a command sees in its environment and which program the shell runs when a name appears in several places.
intro.whyItMatters: Many puzzling failures come down to a variable that was not exported or a name that resolved to the wrong program.

recap.keyIdea: A new process inherits a copy of the exported variables of the shell that started it, and the shell turns a command name into a program by searching the directories of PATH from left to right.

blocks.text: A variable set with name=value belongs to the shell until it is exported, and export copies it to every child, which changes only its own copy. Single quotes keep a dollar sign literal, double quotes let it expand, and $( ) replaces a command with its output.
PATH is a colon-separated list of directories, the first match wins and the current directory is not searched, so a program outside PATH is run with its path, as in ./tool.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson puts commands, variables and exit statuses together in a script: a file of commands with conditions, loops and arguments.

lessons.title: Shell scripts

steps.headline: A script is a text file of commands, with a first line naming the interpreter, made executable and run by its path.

lead.text: Anything you type at a prompt can be saved in a file and run again, and a file of commands is a **script**. Its first line is #!/bin/bash, a line that begins with #! and names the program that is to read the rest, so the system knows how to run it. After that, the commands run one per line, in order. The file has to be executable, which chmod +x gives it, and you run it by its path, as in ./r.sh, because the current directory is not in PATH.

A script runs in a child process, which has two consequences from the last lessons: its variables are not set in the shell that started it, and it hands back an exit status. That is the status of its last command, or the number given to exit, so exit 3 ends the script with status 3, and the shell reads it with $?. The figure steps through making a script executable, running it and reading its status.

diagram.alt: A three-line script r.sh with the lines #!/bin/bash, echo hi and exit 3, next to a terminal. First the file is made executable with chmod +x. Then ./r.sh prints hi. Then echo $? prints 3, the status given by exit 3.
diagram.caption: Making a script executable, running it and reading its status. Use the buttons to step through.

steps.headline: if tests the exit status of a command, and 0 counts as true, so grep -q and [ ] can both drive it.

lead.text: A script needs to make decisions, and the shell's way of doing it is plain. The statement if runs a command and looks at its exit status: if the status is 0 it runs the commands after then, and otherwise it runs those after else, and fi ends the statement. There is no separate idea of a true value. A command that succeeded is true and one that failed is false, which is why you can write if grep -q beta notes.txt, where the option -q makes grep print nothing and only leave its status.

To test a condition that is not a command you know, the shell has a test written between square brackets: [ -f notes.txt ] succeeds if notes.txt is an ordinary file, and [ 3 -gt 2 ] succeeds if 3 is greater than 2. The spaces inside the brackets are required, since [ is itself a command and the brackets are its arguments. A test that fails leaves status 1, and the figure shows the two paths of an if.

diagram.alt: An if statement tests the exit status of a command. If the command exits with status 0, the then branch runs. With any other status the else branch runs.
diagram.caption: An if looks at an exit status, and 0 counts as true. Use the buttons to compare a match and no match.

reveal.text: The test is false, so an if that used it would take its else branch.
The next screen traces two chains in this way, and the figure shows the status after each step.

steps.headline: && runs the next command only after a success and || only after a failure, and a chain is read left to right.

lead.text: A chain is read from left to right, and each operator looks at the exit status left by the command just before it. With A && B, the shell runs B only if A succeeded, and with A || B it runs B only if A failed. A command that is skipped does not run and does not change the status, so the status that follows is still the one from the last command that did run.

That last point is why a chain is not an if with an else. In false || echo A && echo B, false fails, so echo A runs and succeeds, and && then runs echo B, which prints A and B. In true || echo A && echo B, true succeeds, so echo A is skipped, but the status is still 0 from true, and && therefore runs echo B, which prints only B. The figure traces both.

afterFigure.text: For a real choice between two actions use if with else, and keep && and || for a short chain whose steps are easy to see.

diagram.alt: Two traces of a chain of commands. For false || echo A && echo B, false fails, so echo A runs and prints A, and then echo B runs and prints B. For true || echo A && echo B, true succeeds, so echo A is skipped, but the status is still 0, so echo B runs and prints B.
diagram.caption: Each operator looks at the status of what came before it. Use the buttons to compare two chains.

The skipped echo A leaves the status as it was.</text></svg>

reveal.text: Both operators looked at the same success. The && ran its command, and the || did not.

steps.headline: A for loop runs its body once for each word in a list, and the list can come from a glob.

lead.text: A for loop repeats commands once for each word in a list. In for i in 1 2 3 4; do echo $((i*i)); done, the variable i takes each of the four words in turn, and the body runs with it, so the output is the squares 1, 4, 9 and 16. The form $(( )) does arithmetic on whole numbers, so the shell replaces $((i*i)) with the square of i.

The list can be a glob, which the shell expands before the loop starts. In a directory with a.txt, b.txt and c.log, for f in *.txt runs its body twice, once for a.txt and once for b.txt, and never for c.log. A variable inside the body keeps its value from round to round, so a loop can build a total, which the worked example does.

diagram.alt: Two for loops traced round by round. The loop for i in 1 2 3 4 prints 1, 4, 9 and 16, one value per round. The loop for f in *.txt, in a directory with a.txt, b.txt and c.log, runs twice, with f equal to a.txt and then b.txt.
diagram.caption: A for loop runs its body once per word. Use the buttons to compare a list of numbers and a glob.

steps.headline: A script reads its arguments as $1, $2 and so on, counts them in $#, and "$@" gives all of them as separate words.

lead.text: The words that follow a script's name when you run it are its **arguments**, and inside the script they appear as positional parameters: $1 is the first, $2 the second, and $# is how many there are. The form "$@", in quotes, stands for all of them as separate words, each kept whole. So for bash s.sh "a b" c, the count $# is 2, since the quotes made a b one argument, and "$@" is the two words a b and c.

Quote it. Unquoted, $@ is split again at blanks, and a b would become two words, a and b. The same applies to any variable that might hold a name with a space in it. Two habits keep a script from going wrong quietly: quote your variables, and put set -e near the top, which ends the script at the first command that fails, instead of letting it carry on after an error.

diagram.alt: A script s.sh run as bash s.sh with the arguments a b in quotes, and c. The count $# is 2, $1 is a b, $2 is c, and the quoted form of all arguments gives two words. In a loop, the unquoted form splits a b into two words, while the quoted form keeps them together.

steps.headline: Trace count=0; for i in 1 2 3 4; do if [ $i -gt 2 ]; then count=$((count+1)); fi; done; echo $count.

workedSteps.text: count starts at 0. The loop runs four times, with i equal to 1, 2, 3 and 4, and each round tests whether i is greater than 2.
Take i equal to 1. The test [ 1 -gt 2 ] is false. What status does a false test leave?
So the then branch is skipped for i equal to 1 and for 2, and count stays 0.
For i equal to 3 and to 4 the test succeeds, and each round adds 1 to count.
The loop ends and echo prints the final value.

steps.headline: Trace s=0; for i in 1 2 3; do s=$((s+i*i)); done; echo $s.

workedSteps.text: s starts at 0 and each round adds the square of i.
The rounds add 1, then 4, then 9.
Write the number that echo $s prints at the end.

reveal.text: The chain did not stop at the skipped command, because && looks only at the status left behind it.

lessons.orientation: Read a short script and say what it prints and what exit status it returns, using conditions, loops and arguments.
lessons.nextAction: Say how software is installed and kept running on a typical distribution, and find out why a service failed.

blocks.text: The line if grep -q beta notes.txt; then echo found; else echo missing; fi prints found when notes.txt contains the word beta and missing when it does not. Nothing in it compares or calculates: the if runs the command grep -q beta notes.txt, which prints nothing and leaves only an exit status behind, and it chooses its branch by looking at that status.

Every script, however long, is built from decisions and repetitions of this kind, so once you can say what status each command leaves, you can say what a script will print and what status it will end with before you run it. A script is a file of such lines, and reading one comes down to tracing them in order.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say what a short script prints and what exit status it leaves, including chains of && and || and loops over arguments.
intro.whyItMatters: A script is only a list of commands, so every behaviour you meet in one can be traced by the same rules.

recap.keyIdea: A script is a file of commands whose decisions all come from exit statuses, so you can trace one by following the status that each command leaves.

blocks.text: The first line #! names the interpreter, chmod +x makes the file executable, and the script runs in a child process and returns the status of its last command or of exit. if tests a status, 0 meaning true, and && and || are read left to right, each looking at the status of what came just before.
A for loop runs its body once per word, a glob being expanded first, and a script reads its arguments as $1, $2, $# and "$@", which should be quoted so that names with blanks are not split.

recap.nextHook: The last lesson looks at how software gets onto a machine and is kept running: packages, services and the logs that say why one failed.

lessons.title: Packages, services and logs

steps.headline: A package manager installs software together with what it depends on, from signed repositories, and records what is installed.

lead.text: Almost no program stands alone. A web server needs libraries, and those need other libraries, and each has versions that must fit together. Doing that by hand would mean downloading files from several places and tracking them yourself. A **package** is a program bundled with a description of what it depends on, and a **package manager** installs it with those dependencies, keeps a record of what is installed, and removes it cleanly later. On Debian and Ubuntu the tool is apt, and on Fedora and Red Hat it is dnf.

The packages come from **repositories**, servers whose addresses are listed in the system's configuration and whose packages are signed, so the package manager can check that a package is the one the distribution published. sudo apt install nginx therefore does not fetch from any site on the internet. It uses only the configured, signed ones. apt keeps a local list of what the repositories offer: apt update refreshes that list and changes nothing else, and apt upgrade installs the newer versions that the list shows.

afterFigure.text: The figure moves one step along the same path for each command. If apt install says a package cannot be found, the first thing to try is apt update, which refreshes the list that the install reads.

diagram.alt: Three boxes from left to right: a signed repository, the list of available packages on your machine, and the installed software. apt update copies the list from the repository. apt upgrade installs newer versions from the list. apt install nginx installs nginx and the packages it depends on.

reveal.text: Each family of distributions has its own package manager, and the habits that you learn with apt carry over to them.
The next screen explains systemd, and why starting a service now and starting it at boot are separate matters.

steps.headline: systemd starts and supervises services, and starting one now and enabling it at boot are separate settings.

lead.text: The first process the kernel starts, PID 1, is the one that starts everything else, and on most distributions today that is **systemd**, which was first released in 2010 and which Debian made its default init system in release 8 in 2015. It manages **units**, and the commonest kind of unit is a **service**, a long-running program described by a unit file that says what to run, when to start it and what it needs.

You control a service with systemctl. systemctl start and systemctl stop run and end it now, restart does both, and systemctl status shows its state: active when it is running, inactive when it is stopped and failed when it stopped by itself. A different command, systemctl enable, makes it start at every boot, and it does not start the service now. The two settings are independent, and the figure follows a service through them.

afterFigure.text: That independence is the point of the earlier question: start leaves the next boot as it was. enable --now does both in one command, when that is what you want.

diagram.alt: Four states of a service drawn as two boxes, one for right now and one for the next boot. Just installed, it is stopped and not set to start. After systemctl start it is running but not set to start at boot. After systemctl enable it is running and starts at boot. If the program crashes it shows as failed, while still enabled.
diagram.caption: Two separate questions: is it running now, and does it start at boot. Use the buttons to follow a service.

steps.headline: The journal is where systemd keeps the messages of services, and journalctl reads it, one unit at a time with -u.

lead.text: When a service fails, its state tells you that and its log tells you why. systemd collects everything that its services write into the **journal**, which journalctl reads. journalctl -u nginx shows the messages of that one service, -f keeps following the log as new lines arrive, and --since limits it to a time such as "1 hour ago". The last lines are usually the useful ones, since they were written just before the failure.

Not every message is in the journal. Some programs write their own text files under /var/log, which you read with the tools of the earlier lessons, tail and grep among them, and the journal itself is not a plain text file, so journalctl is the way to read it. The figure shows a failure being traced in three steps: the state, the messages, and the fix.

diagram.alt: Three steps to diagnose a failed service called nginx. systemctl status nginx shows Active: failed. journalctl -u nginx shows that nginx could not bind to port 80 because the address was already in use. After the other program is stopped, systemctl start nginx brings the service back to active, running.
diagram.caption: Find the state, then the reason. Use the buttons to step through a failed service.

steps.headline: Diagnose a service nginx that did not come back after a reboot.

workedSteps.text: Ask systemd for the state first, with systemctl status nginx.
The line Active: shows a word. For a service that stopped by itself, which word does it show?
Read its messages with journalctl -u nginx, and look at the last lines.
The last lines say that nginx could not bind to port 80 because the address was in use, so another program holds the port.
Stop the other program, start nginx again and check the state once more.

steps.headline: cron runs commands on a schedule written as five fields, and systemd timers do the same job for units.

lead.text: Some jobs have to run at set times, and the oldest tool for that is cron. A line in a crontab, edited with crontab -e, has five fields and then a command: the **minute**, the hour, the day of the month, the month and the day of the week. A star means every value. So 30 2 * * 1 runs at 02:30 on every Monday, with 1 standing for Monday and 0 for Sunday.

A field can also hold a list, as in 1,3,5, a range, as in 1-5, which includes both ends, or a step, as in */15, which means every fifteenth value. The line 0 6 * * 1-5 therefore runs at 06:00 from Monday to Friday, and */15 * * * * runs at 0, 15, 30 and 45 minutes past every hour. systemd has an equivalent in timers, which start a unit on a schedule and log through the journal.

diagram.alt: Three cron expressions with their five fields labelled: minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week. 30 2 * * 1 means 02:30 every Monday. 0 6 * * 1-5 means 06:00 from Monday to Friday. */15 * * * * means every 15 minutes.

steps.headline: Read 0 6 * * 1-5 field by field, and count the days a week it runs.

workedSteps.text: The minute is 0 and the hour is 6, so the job runs at 06:00.
The day of the month and the month are stars, so they do not limit it. Only the day of the week does.
The range 1-5 covers Monday to Friday. Write the number of days a week.

reveal.text: A step is a short way of listing times, and here it gives an interval that divides the hour exactly.

lessons.orientation: Say how software is installed and kept running on a typical distribution, and find out why a service failed.
lessons.nextAction: You can now read a command line, move around the file tree, join commands with pipes, read permissions and processes, and trace a short script.

blocks.text: The command sudo apt install nginx fetches a web server together with every library it needs, checks that each package is signed by the distribution that published it, and records what it installed so that it can be removed cleanly later. All of that is done by a package manager, and the same few commands work for every program the distribution offers.

A web server also has to keep running once it is installed, and on most Linux machines that is the work of systemd, which starts it, supervises it and keeps what it prints in a journal that you can read when the service fails. Jobs that must happen at set times are the work of cron, and between them these tools let you say where a program came from, whether it is running and why it stopped.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to choose the right package and service command for a task, read a cron line, and find out why a service failed.
intro.whyItMatters: These commands are how software is installed and kept running, and the journal is where a failure explains itself.

recap.keyIdea: A package manager installs software with its dependencies from signed repositories, systemd keeps services running, and the journal and a service's state tell you why one failed.

blocks.text: apt update refreshes the list of available packages and apt upgrade installs newer versions, using only configured, signed repositories. systemctl start runs a service now and systemctl enable makes it start at boot, the two being separate, while systemctl status shows whether it is active, inactive or failed.

journalctl -u followed by the service name shows its messages, and /var/log holds the text logs of programs that write their own. A cron line has five fields, minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week, so 30 2 * * 1 runs at 02:30 every Monday.

questions.prompt:
The line below is typed at the prompt, and its blanks are spaces: one between echo and one, two between one and two, and three between two and three. How many arguments does the program echo receive?

echo one  two   three
hints: Find the words first: a run of blanks between two words is one boundary.
The first word names the program, so it is not one of the arguments.
Count the words that remain after echo.
questions.onCorrect: The shell split the line at runs of blanks, so echo received three separate words.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts echo as well. The first word names the program, and only the words after it are its arguments.
That counts the blanks. The shell uses blanks only to find where one word ends, and the program never sees them.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The shell splits at the blanks into echo, one, two and three. The first word names the program, and the other three are its arguments.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the program that reads the line you type, splits it into words and starts the program named by the first word?
hints: It is a program in its own right, and it runs inside the terminal window.
questions.onCorrect: The shell is a separate program from the terminal window, which only displays text and passes keystrokes along.

misconceptions.feedback: The terminal window only displays text and carries your keystrokes. The program that interprets the line is a separate one.

questions.prompt: Why does sort -rn scores.txt do exactly what sort -r -n scores.txt does?
hints: Think about who reads the letters after the dash: the shell or sort.
questions.onCorrect: Programs that follow this convention read each letter after a single dash as its own option.

misconceptions.feedback: The shell does not rewrite options. It only splits the line, and sort itself reads -rn as the two letters r and n.
The dash is what marks a word as an option. Without it r and n would be taken as names of files.

acceptedIdeas: Single-letter options can be written together after one dash.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Single-letter options can be written together after one dash.

choices.label: The shell joins separate options into one word before sort starts.
sort ignores the dash and reads r and n as file names.
Single-letter options can be written together after one dash.

questions.prompt: How many arguments does ls receive from the line ls -l -a /home /tmp?
hints: Options are arguments that begin with a dash.
Do not count the program name.
Count -l, -a, /home and /tmp.
questions.onCorrect: Options are not delivered separately: ls receives -l and -a in the same list as the two directory names.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts ls, which names the program rather than being one of its arguments.
That counts only the directory names. -l and -a are arguments too, ones that begin with a dash.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: After ls come four words, -l, -a, /home and /tmp, and ls receives every one of them as an argument.

questions.prompt: The file /etc/passwd lists the accounts on a machine. Which numbered manual section describes how that file is laid out?
hints: Sections 1 and 8 describe commands. Which section holds file formats?
The section list runs 1 to 8, with file formats near the middle.
Find the shelf named for file formats in the figure.
questions.onCorrect: man 1 passwd describes the command you run, and man 5 passwd describes the file, so the same word names two pages.

misconceptions.feedback: Section 1 holds commands such as passwd itself. The layout of a file is described in a different section.
Section 8 is for administration commands. File layouts have their own section.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Section 5 covers file formats and conventions, so man 5 passwd describes /etc/passwd.

questions.prompt: useradd is a command that only an administrator normally runs, to create an account. In which numbered section is its page?
hints: Section 1 is for commands any user runs.
Which section is for administration?
It is the highest number on the list.
questions.onCorrect: Section 8 collects the commands an ordinary user rarely needs, which is why man 8 useradd and man 1 passwd sit on different shelves.

misconceptions.feedback: Section 1 is for commands any user runs. Commands meant for the administrator have their own section.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Administration and privileged commands are documented in section 8, so the page is useradd(8).

questions.prompt: The line mkdir  alpha   beta is typed at the prompt, with spaces between the words. How many arguments does mkdir receive?
hints: Ignore the blanks and list the words.
The first word is the program.
Count the words that remain after mkdir.
questions.onCorrect: The extra blanks never reach mkdir, which receives the two words alpha and beta.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts mkdir, which is the program rather than one of its arguments.
That counts blanks. The shell uses them to find where words end and does not pass them on.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: mkdir is the program, and alpha and beta are its two arguments. The extra blanks are lost when the shell splits the line.

questions.prompt: In the line cp -r src dst, a word beginning with a dash such as -r changes what cp does. What is the one-word name for it?
hints: The word is also used for the settings on the screen of a program.
questions.onCorrect: Options are arguments that begin with a dash, and the program reads each one to change its behaviour.

misconceptions.feedback: cp is the command. -r is a word that cp reads to change what it does.

questions.prompt: Which command opens the manual page that describes the layout of the file /etc/hosts?
hints: File formats and conventions are in section 5.
The section number goes before the name.
questions.onCorrect: The section number comes first, then the name, and section 5 holds file formats.

misconceptions.feedback: Section 1 holds commands, and the layout of a file is described in section 5.
Section 8 holds administration commands. A file layout has its own section.
man reads the section number before the page name. Written this way it looks for a page called hosts and another called 5.

questions.prompt: You are in /var/log and run cd .. , where .. means the parent directory. Which directory is the working directory afterwards? Give its path.
hints: Two dots name the directory that contains the one you are in.
questions.onCorrect: The name .. stands for the parent directory, so the answer does not depend on where you have been before.

misconceptions.feedback: That is two levels up. One .. climbs a single level, from log to the directory that holds it.

questions.prompt: You are in /home/ana/projects and run cd ../docs . What does pwd print?
hints: Climb one level first, then go down into docs.
The parent of projects is the directory that holds it.
questions.onCorrect: The .. leaves projects for its parent, /home/ana, and docs is then entered from there.

misconceptions.feedback: docs is not inside projects. The .. leaves projects first, so docs is entered from its parent.

questions.prompt: What does the name .. stand for in a path? Answer in two words.
hints: It names the directory that holds the one you are in.
questions.onCorrect: A path uses .. for the parent directory, and . for the directory you are in, so neither depends on a history of earlier commands.

misconceptions.feedback: It does not mean the place you were before. Its meaning is fixed by the tree, whatever you did earlier.

questions.prompt: You are in /home/ana/projects and run cd ../../bo/notes . What does pwd print?
hints: Climb twice before going down.
After two .. you are in /home.
questions.onCorrect: After two .. the working directory is /home, and bo/notes is then entered from there.

misconceptions.feedback: That climbs only once. Each .. removes one name from the end of the path.

questions.prompt: The file passwd is a list of the accounts on a machine, and an administrator edits it to change them. In which top-level directory would you expect to find it?
hints: Ask what kind of file it is: something an administrator edits to set up the machine.
Settings are neither programs, nor logs, nor a person's own files.
questions.onCorrect: Files that an administrator edits to configure the system live in /etc, and passwd is one of them.

misconceptions.feedback: /home holds each person's own files. A list of accounts that applies to the whole machine is a setting, and settings are kept elsewhere.
/var holds data that changes while the system runs, such as logs. A list of accounts that an administrator edits is a setting, not a record of events.
/usr holds installed programs and their libraries. A list of accounts is data that configures the system, not a program.

questions.prompt: You are in /usr/share/doc. After cd ../../lib , what does pwd print?
hints: Climb two levels from the end of the path.
questions.onCorrect: Two .. remove doc and share, leaving /usr, and lib is then entered from there.

misconceptions.feedback: That climbs only once. Count both .. before going down into lib.

questions.prompt: You are in /home/ana/projects. After cd ../.. , what does pwd print?
hints: Each .. removes the last name from the path.
questions.onCorrect: Each .. climbs one level, and two of them take /home/ana/projects to /home.

misconceptions.feedback: That climbs only one level. There are two .. in the path.

questions.prompt: Where would you expect a program's log files to be written by default?
hints: Log files change as the system runs.
Configuration, programs, home directories and changing data each have a directory.
questions.onCorrect: /var holds data that changes while the system runs, and /var/log is where programs conventionally keep their logs.

misconceptions.feedback: /etc holds configuration that people edit. Files that grow while programs run belong to /var.
/tmp is for temporary files that may be cleared. Logs are kept in a directory meant for data that changes.
/usr/bin holds the programs themselves, not the records they write.

questions.prompt: A directory holds only two files, notes.txt and .hidden. Which names does ls -a print for it?
hints: Plain ls prints notes.txt alone, because it leaves out every name that starts with a dot.
Every directory holds two entries of its own, and names that start with a dot are among those -a adds.
questions.onCorrect: With -a the listing shows every name, so the two files appear together with . and .., which every directory holds.

misconceptions.feedback: -a adds the names that begin with a dot to the listing, so .hidden is printed as well.
-a also shows the two entries that every directory holds, . and .., so they are printed along with the two files.
-a adds names to the plain listing and takes none away, so notes.txt is printed too.

questions.prompt: A listing line reads -rw-r--r-- 2 bo dev 1536 Nov 20 14:45 plan.txt . Which user owns the file?
hints: Look at the fields after the link count.
questions.onCorrect: The owner comes first and the group second, so this file belongs to the user bo and to the group dev.

misconceptions.feedback: dev is the group, which is the field after the owner.

questions.prompt:
notes.txt holds alpha, beta, gamma, delta and epsilon, one per line. The | in the line below hands the output of the command on its left to the command on its right as input. What does the line print?

head -n 2 notes.txt | tail -n 1
hints: head -n 2 passes on the first two lines of the file.
tail -n 1 works on those two lines, not on the whole file.
questions.onCorrect: head passes on alpha and beta, and tail keeps the last of those two, which is beta.

misconceptions.feedback: alpha is the first line head passes on, but tail -n 1 keeps the last line it receives.
tail -n 1 keeps only one line, so one line is printed, however many head passes on.
head -n 2 stops after two lines, so a third line never reaches tail.

questions.prompt: In notes.txt every character takes one byte. The word alpha has five letters, yet its line adds up to 6 bytes. What accounts for the sixth byte?
hints: Think about what ends each line in the file.
The newline is stored in the file like a letter.
questions.onCorrect: The newline is an ordinary character as far as the file is concerned, which is why wc -c counts it.

misconceptions.feedback: wc counts what is stored in the file and adds nothing of its own. The extra byte is in the file, and it is the newline.
notes.txt has one word on each line and no spaces. The extra byte is the newline that ends the line.

acceptedIdeas: The newline character that ends the line is stored as one more byte.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The newline character that ends the line is stored as one more byte.

choices.label: The newline character that ends the line is stored as one more byte.
wc adds one byte to every line when it counts.
A space is stored after every word.

questions.prompt: notes.txt holds alpha, beta, gamma, delta and epsilon, one per line. What does head -n 3 notes.txt | tail -n 1 print?
hints: head -n 3 passes on three lines.
Take the last of those.
questions.onCorrect: head passes on alpha, beta and gamma, and tail keeps the last of the three.

misconceptions.feedback: beta is the second line. head -n 3 passes on three lines, and tail then keeps the third.

questions.prompt: Which single key leaves less and returns you to the prompt?
hints: The word is the first letter of the action.
questions.onCorrect: Inside less, space moves down a screen, a slash starts a search, and q quits.

questions.prompt: A file holds the three lines red, green and blue, but its last line, blue, has no newline after it. How many lines does wc -l report?
hints: wc -l counts one thing in particular.
Count the newline characters, not the words you can see.
Blue is not followed by a newline.
questions.onCorrect: A last line without a newline is missed by wc -l, so the count can be one less than the number of lines you can read.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the lines you can see. wc -l counts newline characters, and blue has none after it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: wc -l counts newline characters, and there are only two, after red and after green, so it reports 2.

questions.prompt: In the listing -rw-r--r-- 1 ana staff 2048 Mar 3 10:12 report.txt, how many bytes is the file?
hints: Find the field that comes after the group.
It is a plain number.
ls -l shows bytes unless it is told otherwise.
questions.onCorrect: ls -l prints the size in bytes. The option -h would show it as 2.0K, but the size is the same.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the link count, the second field. The size comes after the group name.
That is a size in kilobytes. ls -l shows plain bytes unless -h is given.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The size is the fifth field, and ls -l shows it in bytes unless -h is given, so the file is 2048 bytes.

questions.prompt: notes.txt holds alpha, beta, gamma, delta and epsilon, one per line, each ending in a newline. What does wc -c < notes.txt print?
hints: Count the letters of each word.
Each line has one more byte for its newline.
Add the letters and the five newlines.
questions.onCorrect: wc -c counts every byte, so the newlines are included.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the letters. Each of the five lines also ends in a newline, which is a byte.
That is the line count, which is wc -l. The option -c counts bytes.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The words have 5, 4, 5, 5 and 7 letters, which is 26, and the five newlines add 5 more, making 31.

questions.prompt: A log file has ten thousand lines. Which command lets you read it one screen at a time and search inside it?
hints: One of these commands shows a screen and waits for a key.
questions.onCorrect: less reads only what it needs to show, so it opens a very large file at once.

misconceptions.feedback: cat prints the whole file at once, so the first lines scroll out of sight.
head prints only the first lines and then stops, so you cannot move through the rest.
wc counts lines, words and bytes, and does not show the text.

questions.prompt: A directory holds draft.txt and final.txt. You run mv draft.txt final.txt . How many files does the directory hold afterwards?
hints: mv changes the name of a file.
Two files cannot share one name in a directory.
Count the names left once draft.txt has become final.txt.
questions.onCorrect: mv replaces an existing target without asking, so the earlier final.txt is gone and its content cannot be recovered.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats mv as a copy. It renames, and the target name already in use is replaced.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: mv gives draft.txt the name final.txt and replaces the file that had that name, so one file is left, holding the old draft.

questions.prompt: A directory holds file1.txt, file2.txt and file10.txt. Which names does file[1-2].txt match?
hints: A bracket set stands for exactly one character, taken from the set.
[1-2] is the range from 1 to 2, and it must be followed straight away by .txt.
questions.onCorrect: The set matches a single 1 or 2 after file, so file1.txt and file2.txt fit and file10.txt, which has two characters there, does not.

misconceptions.feedback: A bracket set matches exactly one character, and file10.txt has two characters, 1 and 0, between file and .txt.
[1-2] stands for the range from 1 to 2, so it covers both 1 and 2, and file1.txt fits as well.
[1-2] allows one character that is 1 or 2, and file10.txt has two characters in that place, so it cannot fit.

questions.prompt: In an empty directory you run touch holiday photos, with no quotes, and then ls. What does ls list?
hints: The shell finds where one word ends by looking for blanks.
touch makes one file for every name it is given.
questions.onCorrect: The unquoted blank ends the first word, so touch received two names and made two files.

misconceptions.feedback: The shell splits the line at the blank, so touch receives two arguments and makes two files. Only quotes would keep the blank inside one name.
touch is given two ordinary names, holiday and photos, so there is nothing for it to refuse, and it creates both.

choices.label: Nothing, because touch reports an error

questions.prompt: Before ls starts, the pattern in ls *.txt is replaced by the names that match it. Which program does the replacing?
hints: Think about which program reads the line and splits it into words.
questions.onCorrect: The shell expands the pattern before it starts ls, which is why ls receives names and never a star.

misconceptions.feedback: ls only receives the finished list of names. The replacement happens before ls is started, so ls never sees the pattern.
The terminal only displays text and carries keystrokes. It does not look in directories or read patterns.

questions.prompt: The same directory holds file1.txt, file2.txt and file10.txt. How many names does file*.txt match?
hints: The star matches any run of characters, including more than one.
Check each of the three names against the pattern.
Which names begin with file and end with .txt?
questions.onCorrect: A star matches any run of characters, including a longer one such as 10, which is what ? and a bracket set cannot do.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count for ? or a bracket set, which match one character. The star matches a run of any length, so file10.txt also matches.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The star matches any run of characters, so file1.txt, file2.txt and file10.txt all match.

questions.prompt: A directory holds file1.txt, file2.txt and file10.txt, and no file ends in .zip. You run echo *.zip , and echo prints its arguments. What does it print?
hints: The shell replaces a pattern with the names that match it.
Think about what the shell passes on when no name matches.
questions.onCorrect: With no match the shell leaves the pattern as typed, so echo received the text and printed it.

misconceptions.feedback: The shell does not remove a pattern that matches nothing. It passes the pattern on unchanged, so echo has an argument to print.
The shell says nothing about a pattern that matches no names. echo simply receives the text and prints it.
A pattern is replaced only by the names that match it, and none of the three names fits it.

choices.label: An error saying that no file matches
Every file name in the directory

questions.prompt: A directory holds file1.txt, file2.txt and file10.txt. How many names does file?.txt match?
hints: ? stands for exactly one character.
Check how many characters sit between file and .txt in each name.
file10.txt has two.
questions.onCorrect: ? matches one character where * matches any run, which is why the two patterns give different counts.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count for file*.txt. The question mark matches only one character, so file10.txt is left out.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The question mark matches exactly one character, so file1.txt and file2.txt match and file10.txt does not.

questions.prompt: In an empty directory you run touch "my file" , with the quotes, and then ls . How many files does ls list?
hints: Count the arguments touch receives.
Quotes keep the blank inside one word.
One argument creates one file.
questions.onCorrect: Double quotes keep a name with blanks as one argument, but the file name now contains a space that you must quote again every time.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the result without quotes. Quoting keeps the blank inside a single argument.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The quotes keep my file together as one word, so touch creates a single file whose name contains a space.

questions.prompt: final.txt already exists. What does mv draft.txt final.txt do by default?
hints: Think about how mv treats a target that already exists.
The option -i changes the behaviour.
questions.onCorrect: Because the old file is gone with no bin to recover it from, mv -i is the safer form when the target might exist.

misconceptions.feedback: Only mv -i asks first. By default mv replaces the target silently.
mv does not refuse. An existing target is replaced.
mv never combines files. It gives one file the name of the other and replaces the old target.
