questions.prompt: echo 'aXbXc' | sed 's/X/-/' prints a line. How many dashes does it contain?
hints: The pattern X occurs twice in the line.
Without g, sed stops after the first match on a line.
How many of the two X characters are replaced?
questions.onCorrect: Adding g, as in s/X/-/g, replaces every match on the line.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what the g flag would do. Without it, only the first match on a line is replaced.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Without the g flag sed replaces only the first match on each line, so one X becomes a dash.

questions.prompt: In the six-line log the pages are /index, /about, /old, /index, /index and /data. How many lines does cut -d' ' -f3 access.log | sort -u | wc -l print?
hints: -u keeps one copy of each different line.
List the different pages.
Count them.
questions.onCorrect: Counting distinct values is the same pipeline with the counts left out.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every line. sort -u keeps one copy of each different page.
That leaves out one of the four different pages.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: sort -u keeps one copy of each different page, and there are four: /index, /about, /old and /data.

questions.prompt:
printf '10
9
100
' | sort | head -1 prints one line. What is it?
hints: sort compares text, character by character, from the left.
Compare the first characters of the three lines.
When the first characters tie, the shorter line comes first.
questions.onCorrect: In text order 10 comes first, then 100, then 9, which is why sort -n exists.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the smallest number. Without -n the order is by characters, and 1 comes before 9.
The shorter line is a prefix of this one, so it comes first in text order.

questions.prompt:
printf 'a
b
a
' | uniq | wc -l prints how many lines?
hints: uniq compares each line with the one before it.
Are the two a lines next to each other?
Nothing is collapsed.
questions.onCorrect: After sort the two a lines would meet and uniq would leave two lines.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the answer after sort. Without it the two a lines are not neighbours.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: uniq collapses only neighbouring duplicates, and the two a lines are not neighbours, so all three lines remain.

questions.prompt:
printf 'ana,3
bo,5
cy,4
' | awk -F, '{s+=$2} END{print s}' prints what?
hints: -F, sets the separator to a comma.
Field 2 of each line is the number.
Add the three numbers.
questions.onCorrect: The END action runs after all lines have been read, so one total is printed.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the first number only. The action runs for every line and keeps adding to s.
That is the second number only. s accumulates the field from every line.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: -F, makes the comma the separator, so field 2 is 3, 5 and 4, and their sum is 12.

questions.prompt: A mode can be written as three digits, one for the owner, one for the group and one for others. Within a digit, read counts 4, write counts 2 and execute counts 1, and the digit is the total of the bits that are on. Which number is the mode rwxr-xr-- ?
hints: Work out one group at a time: rwx, then r-x, then r--.
The digits are written side by side in the order owner, group, others.
questions.onCorrect: rwx is 4 + 2 + 1, r-x is 4 + 1 and r-- is 4, and the three digits side by side make 754.

misconceptions.feedback: Each group gets a digit of its own, and the three digits are written side by side. They are not added together.
The digits run in the order owner, group, others. The group has r-x, which is 5, and others have r--, which is 4, so the 5 and the 4 are the wrong way round.
A digit is the total of the bits that are on in its group only. The group has no write bit and others have only read, so only the owner's digit is a 7.

questions.prompt: Write the nine-character permission string for mode 640.
hints: Turn each digit into three bits: 4 is read, 2 is write and 1 is execute.
The first digit is for the owner, the second for the group and the last for others.
questions.onCorrect: The digit 6 is read plus write, 4 is read alone and 0 is nothing, so the string is rw- for the owner, r-- for the group and --- for others.

misconceptions.feedback: That is mode 664. Write each digit of 640 as three bits.

questions.prompt: A file has mode 644. After chmod u+x on it, what is its octal mode?
hints: u names the owner, and +x switches on the execute bit.
The owner digit gains the value of execute.
Only the owner's digit changes.
questions.onCorrect: Symbolic modes change only the bits they name and leave the rest as they were.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds execute for others. The letter u names the owner, the first digit.
That adds execute for everyone. u names only the owner.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: u+x adds the execute bit for the owner, which raises the owner's digit from 6 to 7, so the mode is 744.

questions.prompt: You own a file report.txt whose mode is 444, so nobody has write permission on it, and it sits in a directory of yours with mode 755. Can you remove it with rm -f?
hints: A file's name is an entry in a directory.
Ask which of the two, the file or the directory, rm changes.
questions.onCorrect: rm removes the name from the directory, and write permission on the directory allows that, whatever the file's own bits say.

misconceptions.feedback: The file's own bits decide who may read or change its contents. Removing it changes the directory that holds its name, so what matters is write permission on the directory.
There is no such rule. Write permission on the directory decides, and as its owner you have it in mode 755.

acceptedIdeas: Yes, because you may write to the directory that holds it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes, because you may write to the directory that holds it

choices.label: No, because nobody may write to the file
Yes, because you may write to the directory that holds it
No, because only root may remove a read-only file

questions.prompt: A new file starts from mode 666, and the umask is 027. Which octal digit does the group get?
hints: The umask removes bits, digit by digit.
The group digit of the umask is the second one.
Remove its bits from the group digit of the starting mode.
questions.onCorrect: The bits are removed one by one, not subtracted as whole numbers, though here both give the same result.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the digit before the umask is applied. The umask clears the write bit for the group.
That keeps the write bit instead of read. The umask clears write.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The group digit of the umask has the write bit set, and removing write from read plus write leaves read, which is 4.

questions.prompt: With umask 022, what octal mode does a new regular file get? Files start from 666.
hints: The umask digits are 0, 2 and 2.
Clear the write bit from the group and others digits.
The owner digit is untouched.
questions.onCorrect: A umask of 022 gives the common default of readable by everyone and writable by the owner alone.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mode before the umask is applied. The umask clears bits.
That is the mode for a new directory under the same umask. Files start from 666.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The umask clears the write bit for the group and for others, so 666 becomes 644.

questions.prompt: A file has mode 640, belongs to the user ana and the group staff, and bo is a member of staff but is not ana. What may bo do with the file?
hints: The kernel picks the first triplet that applies to the process.
Write out the three triplets of mode 640 and decide which one applies to bo.
questions.onCorrect: bo is not the owner but is in the group, so the group triplet of 640 applies, and that allows reading only.

misconceptions.feedback: A group member is given the group triplet, which in mode 640 is the digit 4. That is the read bit alone, with no write bit.
The kernel uses the group triplet for a member of the group, and in mode 640 that triplet allows reading.

acceptedIdeas: Read it but not write to it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Read it but not write to it

choices.label: Read it and write to it
Nothing, because bo is not the owner
Read it but not write to it

questions.prompt: What is the octal mode of rw-rw-r-- ?
hints: Split the string into three groups of three.
Add the values of the bits that are present in each group.
Write the three sums side by side.
questions.onCorrect: Two groups with read and write make the digit 6 twice, and the others have read alone.

misconceptions.feedback: The others have no write bit in this string, so their digit is smaller.
That gives the owner the execute bit, which the string does not set.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Read plus write is 4 + 2 = 6 for the owner and for the group, and read alone is 4 for others, which gives 664.

questions.prompt: Write the nine-character permission string for mode 751.
hints: Turn each digit into three bits.
The digit 5 is read and execute, and the digit 1 is execute alone.
questions.onCorrect: The owner has all three bits, the group has read and execute, and others have execute only.

misconceptions.feedback: That gives the others read and execute. The last digit is the smaller one.

questions.prompt: With umask 077, what octal mode does a new regular file get? Files start from 666.
hints: Clear every bit that the group and others digits of the umask contain.
The umask digit 7 has all three bits.
Only the owner's digit survives.
questions.onCorrect: A umask of 077 is the usual way to keep new files private to their owner.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mode before the umask is applied.
Files start from 666, so the owner has no execute bit to keep.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The umask clears every bit for the group and for others, so only the owner's read and write remain, which is 600.

questions.prompt: The command line is: sleep 1 & echo P; wait; echo Q . It prints two lines. What is the first one?
hints: The & puts sleep in the background, so the shell carries on at once.
wait comes after the first echo.
questions.onCorrect: The background job does not hold the shell back, so echo P runs at once, and wait then pauses the shell until sleep ends.

questions.prompt: Ending a command with & starts it in the background, so the shell carries on without waiting for it to finish. You type sleep 5 & echo P . When does P appear?
hints: The & tells the shell not to wait for the command it follows.
Ask what the shell does after it has started the sleep.
questions.onCorrect: The sleep runs in the background, so the shell is free at once and echo P runs without delay.

misconceptions.feedback: Because of the &, the shell does not wait for the sleep. It goes straight on to the next command.
The & ends the first command, and the shell goes on to run the second. Both commands on the line are run.

acceptedIdeas: Straight away, while the sleep carries on in the background
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Straight away, while the sleep carries on in the background

choices.label: Straight away, while the sleep carries on in the background
After five seconds, once the sleep has ended
Never, because the shell runs only the first command on a line

questions.prompt: Which key combination suspends the program running in the foreground without ending it? Write it as Ctrl- and a letter.
hints: It is not the combination that interrupts a program.
questions.onCorrect: Ctrl-Z sends SIGTSTP, which suspends the program, and bg or fg then resumes it in the background or the foreground.

misconceptions.feedback: Ctrl-C sends SIGINT, which usually ends the program. A different key suspends it.

questions.prompt: Which of these signals can a program neither catch nor ignore?
hints: One signal is acted on by the kernel without asking the program.
questions.onCorrect: Because SIGKILL cannot be caught, a program gets no chance to clean up, so SIGTERM is the one to send first.

misconceptions.feedback: A program can catch SIGTERM, which is why it is a polite request to finish.
A program can catch SIGINT, and many do, to clean up before they stop.
A program can catch SIGHUP, and some use it to reread their configuration.

questions.prompt: In sleep 1 & echo started; wait; echo done , how many background jobs does wait have to wait for?
hints: Count the commands that end in &.
Only those are background jobs.
The echo commands run in the foreground.
questions.onCorrect: With no argument, wait pauses until every background job of the shell has finished.

misconceptions.feedback: Only the sleep was started in the background. The echo commands ran in the foreground.
The sleep was started with &, so it is a background job that wait must wait for.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only one job was started with &, which is sleep 1, so wait has one job to wait for.

questions.prompt: { sleep 1; echo A; } & echo B; wait; echo C prints three lines. What is the second one? Give the letter.
hints: The group in braces runs in the background and waits one second before it prints.
B is printed at once.
wait pauses the shell until the group has finished.
questions.onCorrect: wait holds back echo C until the background group has finished, so A comes before C and after B.

misconceptions.feedback: wait holds echo C back until the background group, which prints A, has finished.
B is printed at once, so it comes first, and the second line is the one that waited a second.

questions.prompt: In bash, sleep 10 & kill -9 $! ; wait $! ; echo $? prints the exit status of the killed job. A process ended by signal N reports the status 128 plus N. What is printed?
hints: kill -9 sends the signal whose number is 9.
The status for death by a signal is 128 plus the number.
Add the two numbers.
questions.onCorrect: kill with no option would send 15 and give 143, so the status tells you which signal ended a process.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the signal number. The status adds 128 to it when a process is ended by a signal.
A process ended by a signal does not report success. Its status is 128 plus the signal number.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The signal sent was SIGKILL, number 9, and the status of a process ended by a signal is 128 plus its number, which is 137.

questions.prompt: What signal number does kill -9 send?
hints: The number after the dash is the signal number.
Which signal cannot be caught?
The answer is the number written in the option.
questions.onCorrect: SIGKILL always has the number 9, on every Linux architecture.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the signal that kill sends when no option is given. The option here names another one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The option -9 names the signal by number, and 9 is SIGKILL.

questions.prompt: What signal number does kill 4321 send, with no option?
hints: Think about the default signal of kill.
It is the one a program is allowed to catch.
Its name begins with SIGT.
questions.onCorrect: SIGTERM is the polite request, and -9 is the last resort when the program ignores it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the signal sent only when you write -9. The default can be caught by the program.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: With no option, kill sends SIGTERM, which is signal 15, a request to finish that the program may handle.

questions.prompt: sleep 1 & echo started; wait; echo done prints two lines. What is the first line?
hints: The & puts sleep in the background.
Does anything hold back the first echo?
questions.onCorrect: wait pauses the shell only at its own position in the line, so echo started has already run.

misconceptions.feedback: echo done comes after wait, which waits for the sleep to finish.

questions.prompt: In a shell you type greeting=hi , with no export. You then run bash -c 'echo [$greeting]' , which starts a new shell as a child and prints the value of greeting between two brackets. What does it print?
hints: bash -c starts a new shell as a child process.
Ask which variables a child receives from its parent.
questions.onCorrect: The variable exists only in the shell where it was set, so the child's $greeting is empty and the brackets close on nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: greeting=hi sets the variable in the first shell only. A child receives a copy of the exported variables, and this one was never exported.
The single quotes stop the first shell from expanding $greeting, but the child shell expands it itself, finds nothing and prints nothing in its place.
An unset variable is not an error in the shell. It expands to nothing, so the brackets enclose an empty string.

acceptedIdeas: Empty brackets, [], with nothing between them
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Empty brackets, [], with nothing between them

choices.label: Empty brackets, [], with nothing between them

questions.prompt: After x=5 and export x , what does bash -c 'echo [$x]' print?
hints: export copies the variable into every child that starts afterwards.
questions.onCorrect: The child starts with a copy of the value that x had when it was started.

misconceptions.feedback: After export, the variable is part of the environment that a child inherits.

questions.prompt: After name=ana and export name , a child runs name=bo . How many separate copies of the variable name exist?
hints: The child got a copy when it started.
The shell keeps its own variable.
Count the shell and the child.
questions.onCorrect: The two copies are independent, so a change in the child cannot reach the shell.

misconceptions.feedback: There would be one only if the child and the shell shared a variable. The child received a copy.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The shell has its own variable and the child has a copy, so the child's change touches one of two.

questions.prompt: n=$(echo hello | wc -c) runs the inner command and stores its output in n. What does echo "$n" print?
hints: wc -c counts bytes, and echo adds a newline.
hello has five letters.
Add the newline.
questions.onCorrect: The shell removes the trailing newline of the substituted output, so n holds the number alone.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the letters. echo adds a newline, which is a byte too.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The inner command prints the byte count, which is six, and the substitution puts that text in place of the $( ), so n holds 6.

questions.prompt: n=4 is set. What does echo '$n' "$n" print?
hints: Single quotes pass the text exactly.
Double quotes let the dollar sign expand.
questions.onCorrect: Single quotes stop the expansion, and double quotes allow it, which is the one difference between them that matters here.

misconceptions.feedback: Single quotes stop the expansion, so the first word is the text $n unchanged.

questions.prompt: PATH is /usr/local/bin:/usr/bin and both directories hold an executable called python. Which directory's copy runs when you type python? Give the directory.
hints: The shell searches the list from the left.
questions.onCorrect: The shell stops at the first directory that holds a match, so the order of PATH decides.

misconceptions.feedback: The shell tries the left-hand directory first, and stops when it finds a match.

questions.prompt: A script called tool sits in your current directory, which is not in PATH. Typing tool alone gives command not found. Why?
hints: Think about where the shell looks when it has to turn a name into a program.
To run the script from here you would give its path, as in ./tool.
questions.onCorrect: The shell searches only the directories in PATH, so a program in the current directory is found only if you give its path, as in ./tool.

misconceptions.feedback: A missing execute bit gives Permission denied once the shell has found the file. command not found means the shell never found a file by that name to run.
The shell does not search the current directory for commands unless it is listed in PATH, and a name's ending plays no part in the search.

acceptedIdeas: The shell looks only in the directories listed in PATH, and the current directory is not one of them
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The shell looks only in the directories listed in PATH, and the current directory is not one of them

choices.label: The file has no execute permission
The shell searches the current directory only for names that end in .sh
The shell looks only in the directories listed in PATH, and the current directory is not one of them

questions.prompt: PATH is /usr/bin:/usr/local/bin, and both directories hold an executable called python. Which directory's copy runs when you type python?
hints: The shell tries the left-hand directory first.
questions.onCorrect: Reversing the list reverses which copy wins, which is how a person puts their own tools ahead of the system's.

misconceptions.feedback: That was the answer when it was listed first. The list is now the other way round.

questions.prompt: x=5 is set in the shell without export. What does bash -c 'echo [$x]' print?
hints: A new bash starts as a child process.
An unexported variable is not copied to it.
questions.onCorrect: The child sees no x, so the dollar-x expands to nothing and only the brackets are printed.

misconceptions.feedback: The variable is not exported, so the child does not receive it.

questions.prompt: x=3 is set. What does echo '$x' "$x" print?
hints: Single quotes pass the text exactly.
Double quotes let the dollar sign expand.
questions.onCorrect: The single quotes keep the text $x, and the double quotes let the shell replace it with the value.

misconceptions.feedback: Single quotes stop the expansion, so the first word is not replaced.
Double quotes still expand the variable, so the second word becomes the value.

questions.prompt: PATH is /opt/a:/opt/b and both directories contain an executable named tool. Which one runs when you type tool?
hints: The shell reads PATH from left to right.
It stops at the first match.
questions.onCorrect: The order of PATH is therefore the order of priority, and a directory placed first overrides the same name later in the list.

misconceptions.feedback: The shell tries directories from left to right, so the one listed first wins.
The shell runs the first match and stops looking.
The shell does not report ambiguity. It uses the first match.

choices.label: Both run, one after the other
None, because the name is ambiguous

questions.prompt: The test [ -f nope ] asks whether nope is an ordinary file, and no such file exists. After it runs, echo $? prints which number?
hints: A test that is false leaves a nonzero status.
The file does not exist.
The number is the one a failing command usually leaves.
questions.onCorrect: A test is a command like any other, and if only looks at the status it leaves.

misconceptions.feedback: Zero means that the test succeeded. Here the file does not exist, so the test fails.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The test fails, so it leaves a nonzero status, and the status a failed test leaves is one.

questions.prompt: In a chain, && runs the next command only after a success and || runs it only after a failure, and the chain is read from left to right. What does false && echo X || echo Y print?
hints: Start with false: it leaves a failure status.
Ask what status the chain has when it reaches the ||, given that echo X was skipped.
questions.onCorrect: && skips echo X after the failure, the failure is still the latest status, and || therefore runs echo Y.

misconceptions.feedback: false fails, so && does not run echo X, and X is never printed.
echo X is skipped because false fails, so X cannot be printed, and only one of the two echo commands can run.
The skipped echo X leaves the failure of false as the latest status, and || runs its command after a failure, so echo Y does run.

questions.prompt: What does true && echo X || echo Y print?
hints: The && runs its right-hand side after a success.
After echo X the status is zero, and || runs only after a failure.
questions.onCorrect: true succeeds, so echo X runs and succeeds, and || therefore skips echo Y.

misconceptions.feedback: The || runs only after a failure, and echo X succeeds, so it does not run the other command.

questions.prompt: What does [ 1 -gt 2 ] leave in $? , given that 1 is not greater than 2?
hints: A false test leaves a nonzero status.
The number is the usual failure status.
It is not zero.
questions.onCorrect: An if treats this nonzero status as false and so skips its then branch.

misconceptions.feedback: Zero would mean that the test passed. The comparison is false.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The test is false, so it leaves a nonzero status, which is one.

questions.prompt: s=0; for i in 1 2 3; do s=$((s+i*i)); done; echo $s prints a number. What is it?
hints: The body adds the square of i each round.
The squares of 1, 2 and 3 are needed.
Add them up.
questions.onCorrect: The variable keeps its value from round to round, so the loop builds a total.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 1, 2 and 3. The body adds the square of i.
That is the last square only. s keeps the sum of every round.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The loop adds the squares 1, 4 and 9 to s, which gives 14.

questions.prompt: What does true || echo A && echo B print? Write the letters in order, separated by a space.
hints: || skips its right-hand side after a success.
What status does the skipped part leave?
&& then looks at that status.
questions.onCorrect: The skipped command does not change the status, so && sees success and runs echo B.

misconceptions.feedback: echo A is skipped, because true succeeded, and || runs its right-hand side only after a failure.
echo A is skipped. true succeeded, and || runs only after a failure.

questions.prompt: What does false || echo A && echo B print? Write the letters in order, separated by a space.
hints: false fails, so || runs the next command.
Then look at the status that echo A leaves, and at what && does with it.
questions.onCorrect: The chain is read left to right, and each operator looks at the status left by what came just before it.

misconceptions.feedback: && runs echo B after echo A succeeds, so the chain does not stop after the first letter.
false fails, so || does run echo A, and nothing stops the chain after that.

questions.prompt: A script s.sh contains only the line echo $# , which prints how many arguments the script received. What does bash s.sh "a b" c print?
hints: Quotes group words into one argument.
How many arguments does the script receive?
Count the groups.
questions.onCorrect: The count is of arguments, not of words, so quoting changes it.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the words. The quotes make a b a single argument.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The quotes keep a b together as one argument, so the script receives two arguments.

questions.prompt: notes.txt exists and contains no line with zzz. After grep -q zzz notes.txt , what status is left in $? ?
hints: grep reports its result in its status.
The file was read without any error.
No match has a status of its own.
questions.onCorrect: The status 2 would mean an error, such as a missing file, so a script can tell no match from a failure.

misconceptions.feedback: Zero means a match was found. There is none.
That means an error, such as a file that cannot be read. Here the search simply found nothing.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: grep exits with 0 when it found a match, with 1 when it found none, and with 2 on an error, so here the status is 1.

questions.prompt: Debian and Ubuntu use apt as their package manager. Which command does Fedora use?
hints: Fedora and Red Hat use the same family of tools.
The name is three letters, and it replaced an older tool called yum.
questions.onCorrect: Different distributions use different package managers, but each installs from signed repositories and tracks what it installed.

misconceptions.feedback: rpm installs single packages and does not fetch what they depend on. The tool that fetches them is a layer above it.

questions.prompt: A service is a program that runs in the background for a long time, such as a web server. On a fresh machine you run systemctl start nginx and then reboot. What state is nginx in after the reboot, with no other command typed?
hints: A service can be started now and, separately, set to start at every boot.
Ask which command you typed, and what it says about the next boot.
questions.onCorrect: start runs the service now and leaves the next boot as it was, so nginx stays stopped until something starts it.

misconceptions.feedback: systemctl start runs the service now and changes nothing about the next boot. Starting at boot is a separate setting.
A reboot stops services in an orderly way. The state failed means that a service stopped by itself with an error.

acceptedIdeas: Not running, because start does not make the service start at boot
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Not running, because start does not make the service start at boot

choices.label: Running, because start also makes the service start at boot
Not running, because start does not make the service start at boot
Failed, because the reboot ended it abruptly

questions.prompt: Which word follows systemctl to make a service start at every boot? Give the single word.
hints: It is the verb that sets the boot behaviour.
questions.onCorrect: enable sets what happens at boot, and enable --now does that and also starts the service at once.

misconceptions.feedback: start runs it now, but it does not change what happens at the next boot.

questions.prompt: Which journalctl option selects the messages of one service, as in journalctl followed by the option and nginx? Give the option.
hints: It stands for the unit, which is the thing systemd manages.
questions.onCorrect: A service is one kind of unit, so the option that picks a unit picks a service's messages.

misconceptions.feedback: -f follows the log as new lines arrive. The option that selects one service has another letter.

questions.prompt: systemctl status shows the word active for a service that is running. Which word does it show for one that stopped because it crashed?
hints: The word describes the outcome of the service.
questions.onCorrect: failed means the service stopped without being asked to, and the journal then holds the reason.

misconceptions.feedback: inactive means that the service is stopped, which a person may have done on purpose. A crash has a name of its own.

questions.prompt: A cron line is 0 6 * * 1-5 , with the range 1-5 in the day-of-week field. How many days a week does it run?
hints: A range covers every value from the first number to the last.
Count the days from the first to the last.
Count from Monday to Friday.
questions.onCorrect: A range is inclusive, so both ends count, and the line runs at 06:00 on each of the five days.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out one end of the range. A range includes both numbers.
That would be every day of the week. The field holds only a range of weekdays.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The range 1-5 covers Monday to Friday, which is five days, and the job runs once on each of them.

questions.prompt: A cron line has */15 in its minute field and * in the others. At which minutes past the hour does it run?
hints: */15 means every fifteenth value of the field.
The minute field starts at 0.
questions.onCorrect: The step runs through the minutes from 0 in jumps of fifteen, so the job runs four times an hour.

misconceptions.feedback: A step repeats through the whole range of the field, so it gives every fifteenth value and not a single one.
The step starts from the first value of the field, which for minutes is 0, so the job also runs at the top of the hour.

questions.prompt: Which command reads the log messages that systemd keeps, including those of services? Give the command name.
hints: The messages are kept in the journal.
questions.onCorrect: journalctl reads the journal, and -u narrows it to one unit, such as journalctl -u nginx.

misconceptions.feedback: cat prints a file, and the journal is not one plain text file that cat can show.

questions.prompt: What does apt update do?
hints: It touches the list, not the software.
Which command installs newer versions?
questions.onCorrect: Run update first so that the list is current, and then upgrade or install uses that list.

misconceptions.feedback: That is apt upgrade. update only refreshes the list of what is available.
Removing unused packages is a different command, apt autoremove.
Neither happens. update changes only the list, and nothing on the system is replaced.

acceptedIdeas: Refreshes the list of available packages
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Refreshes the list of available packages

choices.label: Refreshes the list of available packages
Installs the newest version of every installed package
Removes packages that are no longer needed
Downloads the packages and restarts the services

questions.prompt: What does the cron line 30 2 * * 1 mean?
hints: Name the five fields from the left.
Which field holds the 1?
questions.onCorrect: The last field is the day of the week, where 1 is Monday, so the job runs once a week at 02:30.

misconceptions.feedback: The fields are minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week, so 30 is a minute and 2 is an hour.
The first day of the month would be in the third field. The last field is the day of the week.
The first field is minutes, not seconds, and the last field limits the job to one weekday.

choices.label: Every 30 minutes on 2 days of the week
02:30 on the first day of every month

flashcards.front: What is the program called that reads a command line, splits it at the blanks and starts the program named first?
flashcards.back: The shell reads the line and starts the program; the terminal window only displays text.

flashcards.front: How many arguments does echo receive from: echo a  b   c
flashcards.back: Three: a, b and c; the shell splits at runs of blanks and the program never sees the gaps.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three: a, b and c; the shell splits at runs of blanks and the program never sees the gaps.

flashcards.front: Why is ls -l the same program as ls, and not a different one?
flashcards.back: The program is the first word, and -l is only an argument that changes what that one program does.

flashcards.front: Which two characters name the parent directory in a path?
flashcards.back: Two dots name the parent directory, so the path does not depend on which place you were in earlier.

flashcards.front: Which top-level directory holds log files, as /var/log?
flashcards.back: Data that changes while the system runs, such as logs, lives under /var.

flashcards.front: Why is there no drive letter on a Linux system?
flashcards.back: There is one tree starting at /, and another disk is attached to a directory in it.

flashcards.front: Which command shows one screen of a file at a time and lets you search it?
flashcards.back: less is a pager: space moves down, a slash starts a search and q quits.

flashcards.front: In what unit does ls -l show the size column?
flashcards.back: Bytes, unless -h is added, which prints a rounded size such as 2.0K.

flashcards.front: A file ends in a line with no newline. The file shows 4 lines when read. What does wc -l report if the first three lines have newlines?
flashcards.back: wc -l counts newlines, and only three exist, so it reports 3.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: wc -l counts newlines, and only three exist, so it reports 3.

flashcards.front: What is the name for a pattern such as *.txt that the shell expands to file names?
flashcards.back: A glob is expanded by the shell before the program starts, so the program receives a list of names.

flashcards.front: The directory holds a.txt, b.txt and c.log. How many lines does ls *.txt | wc -l print?
flashcards.back: The shell expands *.txt to a.txt and b.txt, so ls lists two names.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The shell expands *.txt to a.txt and b.txt, so ls lists two names.

flashcards.front: Why can a file removed with rm not be fetched from a rubbish bin?
flashcards.back: rm unlinks the file straight away, so there is no bin in the shell to hold it.

flashcards.front: What do the names in a directory point at?
flashcards.back: A directory entry maps a name to an inode, which holds the metadata and the location of the data.

flashcards.front: A file has one name and you add a hard link. What link count does ls -l show?
flashcards.back: Each name counts, so the original name and the new one make 2.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each name counts, so the original name and the new one make 2.

flashcards.front: Why does a symbolic link break when its target is removed, and a hard link does not?
flashcards.back: A symbolic link stores a path and follows it, while a hard link is another name for the inode itself.

flashcards.front: Which standard stream carries a program's error messages? Give its name.
flashcards.back: Standard error carries error messages, which a pipe or > does not capture unless 2>&1 is added.

flashcards.front: Which operator appends output to a file instead of replacing it?
flashcards.back: > truncates the file first, and >> adds to the end.

flashcards.front: Why does the second program in a pipe not wait for the first to finish?
flashcards.back: Both start together, and the second reads bytes as they arrive until the first closes the pipe.

flashcards.front: Which grep option prints the number of matching lines instead of the lines?
flashcards.back: -c counts lines, and -v inverts the match.

flashcards.front: What exit status does grep return when it finds no match?
flashcards.back: 0 means a match, 1 means none, and 2 means an error.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 0 means a match, 1 means none, and 2 means an error.

flashcards.front: When do you reach for find and when for grep?
flashcards.back: find chooses files by name, type, size or age; grep chooses lines by the text they contain.

flashcards.front: Which two characters anchor a pattern to the start and the end of a line?
flashcards.back: ^ matches the start of the line and $ the end, so a pattern with both must match the whole line.

flashcards.front: Which repetition operator means one or more of the previous item?
flashcards.back: + needs at least one repeat, * allows none and ? allows at most one.

flashcards.front: Why does the glob *.txt differ from the pattern a.*b in grep?
flashcards.back: In a glob the star stands for any characters, but in a regular expression it repeats the previous item.

flashcards.front: Which sort option orders lines as numbers instead of text?
flashcards.back: Without -n, sort compares characters, so 100 comes before 9.

flashcards.front: Which command, given sorted input, prefixes each distinct line with its count?
flashcards.back: uniq -c collapses neighbouring equal lines and writes the count in front.

flashcards.front: Why must the input of uniq be sorted first?
flashcards.back: uniq compares each line only with the one before it, so equal lines that are not neighbours are not collapsed.

flashcards.front: Which octal digit stands for read, write and execute together?
flashcards.back: Read is 4, write is 2 and execute is 1, and 4 + 2 + 1 = 7.

flashcards.front: What octal mode is rw-r--r-- ?
flashcards.back: The owner has read and write for a digit of 6, and the group and others have read alone, 4 each.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The owner has read and write for a digit of 6, and the group and others have read alone, 4 each.

flashcards.front: Why does deleting a file need write permission on the directory, not on the file?
flashcards.back: A file's name is an entry in the directory, so removing it changes the directory.

flashcards.front: Which signal number does kill send when you give it no option?
flashcards.back: SIGTERM is 15, a request that the program may catch.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: SIGTERM is 15, a request that the program may catch.

flashcards.front: Which signal cannot be caught or ignored by a program? Give its name.
flashcards.back: SIGKILL is acted on by the kernel, so the program has no chance to clean up.

flashcards.front: Why does Ctrl-Z not end a program?
flashcards.back: It sends a signal that suspends the program, and bg or fg resumes it.

flashcards.front: Which command copies a shell variable into the environment of the programs it starts?
flashcards.back: export marks a variable so that children inherit a copy.

flashcards.front: What separates the directories in PATH?
flashcards.back: PATH is a list of directories joined by colons, searched from left to right.

flashcards.front: Why does changing a variable in a child not change it in the shell?
flashcards.back: The child works on its own copy, and nothing is copied back to the process that started it.

flashcards.front: What is the first line of a script that names the interpreter called?
flashcards.back: A line starting #! names the program that will run the file, so the system knows how to read it.

flashcards.front: What status does a successful command leave in $?
flashcards.back: By convention 0 means success and anything else means failure.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: By convention 0 means success and anything else means failure.

flashcards.front: Why should "$@" be quoted in a script?
flashcards.back: Quotes keep each argument whole, so a name with a blank is not split into two words.

flashcards.front: Which command shows whether a service is running, stopped or failed?
flashcards.back: systemctl status shows the state, and journalctl -u gives the messages that explain a failure.

flashcards.front: Which systemctl command makes a service start at boot?
flashcards.back: enable sets the boot behaviour, and start only runs the service now.

flashcards.front: Why does apt install not download from just any website?
flashcards.back: It uses only the repositories that are configured, and it checks their signatures.
